articles.title: ‘Agents are very harsh customers’: Microsoft exec warns many apps will lose pricing leverage
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Charles Lamanna , the Microsoft executive who oversees Microsoft 365 and the platform behind Copilot, says most business software will end up running behind AI agents rather than in front of users. That’s bad news for a lot of apps.

“If my agent interacts with your app exclusively, the agent’s your customer, not the end user,” Lamanna said Wednesday morning, speaking with Madrona’s Matt McIlwain in the opening keynote at the venture capital firm’s annual IA40 Summit in Seattle . “And agents are very harsh customers.”

Agents will pick whatever service is cheapest, fastest and most reliable, he said, and they’ll move people to another one quickly. Apps that sit behind agents will have a hard time holding on to pricing power or customer loyalty.

Microsoft’s own apps aren’t exempt. Word, Excel and PowerPoint won’t go away, Lamanna said, but most people will use them inside Copilot, which can now run Office without switching apps. In his view, the standard setup for an office worker ends up as Copilot for AI and Teams for communication, “and that’s maybe it.”

He compared a headless app to a company that sells only on Amazon. It can be a business, he said, but prices get squeezed when buyers are simply choosing between “your pencils or those pencils.” A brand such as Nike has more leverage.

Amazon itself is resisting that role. Earlier this week it blocked Meta’s Muse agent from shopping on its site, saying Meta never asked permission and that the agent doesn’t identify itself and appears to store customer credentials. Meta has said Muse can’t see users’ passwords or payment methods. Amazon is also in a legal fight with Perplexity over that company’s Comet shopping agent.

Amazon is open to agents on its own terms. Days after blocking Muse, it opened its seller tools to Anthropic’s Claude, letting merchants manage inventory, prices and listings without going into Seller Central.
Lamanna brought up Muse himself onstage, predicting it will reach far more people than work-focused agent tools such as Copilot and Claude Cowork.

Microsoft is on the other side of the same question. Copilot depends on other companies’ software being willing to work behind it. In an August profile , Lamanna said Copilot uses connectors to pull data from services such as Salesforce and ServiceNow, so people don’t have to leave the app.

articles.title: There’s a new No. 1 on the GeekWire 200 as AI and hardware reshape our Pacific Northwest startup index
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Companies building software for the AI boom and advanced machinery for space, energy and defense are remaking the Pacific Northwest’s tech economy, and both trends are showing up in full force on the GeekWire 200 , our ranking of the region’s top privately held tech startups.

The Fall 2026 update, released Wednesday morning, features a new No. 1: Temporal, the Bellevue, Wash., company whose software keeps AI agents running reliably. It raised $550 million this month at a $12.55 billion valuation, more than double its value earlier this year. Its annualized revenue has passed $250 million, up more than 200% in a year, with customers including OpenAI, Nvidia and Netflix.

Temporal replaces fusion company Helion, now No. 2. Helion grew its Series G round to $500 million and opened a Seattle office as its headcount topped 800, but questions have emerged about its timeline for delivering fusion power to Microsoft by 2028.
Six of the top 10 companies build advanced machinery: fusion reactors, rockets, drones, radar, military vehicles and weed-zapping robots. Several of them spent the quarter scaling up production.

The GeekWire 200 combines objective data, editorial insight and AI analysis of our coverage to provide a broad view of the region’s startup landscape. Dating to 2013, it has long served as a resource for investors, job seekers, service providers and others tracking the regional tech scene.
See the updated GeekWire 200 , and continue reading for highlights. Here’s the new top 10.

articles.title: Spending management company Fraxion acquires Yellow Dog Software
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: Seattle-based spending management company Fraxion has acquired Yellow Dog Software, which offers inventory management software for the hospitality, sports, food and beverage, and retail industries. Fraxion serves as a digital gatekeeper for business expenses by tracking, controlling and approving business expenses.
Yellow Dog will continue operating out of its Norfolk, Virginia, office and has 67 employees. Terms of the deal were not released.

“Yellow Dog extends Fraxion’s capabilities beyond procure-to-pay into inventory management, adding greater visibility into the downstream impact of purchasing decisions,” Stanton Jandrell, co-founder and CEO of Fraxion, said in a statement.
Fraxion originally launched in South Africa in 1997 and relocated its U.S. headquarters to Seattle in 2019 following its merger with eRequester. It still operates an office in Cape Town.

Last year, private equity firm Main Capital Partners took a majority stake in Fraxion. As part of that transaction, Fraxion also acquired accounts payable provider Centreviews. Fraxion currently has a 69-person headcount, according to the company.

articles.title: Meet the X-BAT: Full specs on the new AI-piloted fighter jet to be built in Washington state
articles.author: John Cook
paras: Traditional military air operations rely heavily on fixed, vulnerable targets: long concrete runways and aircraft carriers.

Shield AI’s new X-BAT autonomous fighter jet is designed to bypass that infrastructure entirely, utilizing a vertical takeoff mechanism and a mobile launch trailer that can operate from highways, remote outposts or standard cargo ships.

Operated without a human in the cockpit, the aircraft relies on aboard algorithms to navigate and execute strike missions where GPS and satellite communications are jammed. The X-BAT has yet to make its maiden flight, but Shield AI and GE Aerospace cleared a critical milestone this summer by completing ground engine tests and integrating the jet’s F110 thrust-vectoring nozzle.
With news that the X-BAT will be mass produced in the Seattle area — bringing 4,000 jobs to the region by the early 2030s — we decided to take a closer look at this groundbreaking aircraft.

articles.title: Shield AI selects Seattle area to build X-BAT autonomous fighter jet, plans to add 4,000 jobs by early 2030s
articles.author: John Cook
paras: DES MOINES, Wash. — Defense tech powerhouse Shield AI is establishing a massive advanced manufacturing hub in Washington state, tapping the Seattle region’s deep aerospace and tech roots to build a next-generation autonomous fighter jet called the X-BAT.

The project could transform the regional labor market: Shield AI says it expects to have 4,000 workers in the region by the early 2030s as it ramps up mass production of the AI-piloted, 26-foot long aircraft.

It marks a major expansion of advanced aerospace manufacturing in the Seattle region, bringing autonomous military aviation directly into Boeing’s backyard and cementing the state’s position at the center of the AI-defined defense era.

The San Diego-based company, valued at $12.7 billion following a $2 billion venture capital round earlier this year, is looking to complete construction on a 420,000-square-foot facility in Des Moines, Wash., just south of Seattle, next spring.

That physical footprint is expected to grow quickly. Armor Harris , senior vice president of aircraft at Shield AI, told GeekWire that the company is actively looking to add another 1 million square feet in the region to support its long-term manufacturing push.

Named X-Forge 3, the initial facility will serve as the primary manufacturing and engineering center for the X-BAT. It’s now under construction about 15 minutes south of Sea-Tac airport in the Des Moines Creek Business Park West, at 1800 S 216th St.
Developed by Panattoni , the site was selected by Shield AI midway through construction. The company is now taking it to completion, with Harris noting that they are “putting the roof on right now.”

Unveiled last year, the X-BAT is an AI-piloted strike fighter that takes off and lands vertically, carries up to 2,000-pound class weapons in internal bays, and is designed for a 1,000-nautical-mile combat radius — which, when it takes flight, would top the estimated 590 nautical mile combat radius of the Lockheed Martin F-35A.

An economic analysis released by the company estimates Shield AI’s X-BAT program will inject roughly $73 billion into Washington state’s economy over the next two decades as production scales toward full capacity. Projections provided by the company say up to 27,000 direct and indirect jobs — including suppliers — will be generated by the expansion by 2046.

“This is a large program,” said Harris in an interview with GeekWire. “Building a next generation fighter jet is no small endeavor, and with the amount of interest that we’ve seen, both from our U.S. government customers and from international customers, we could be looking at building these at rates greater than fighter jets have been built in a really long time.”
Harris said he expects the first X-BAT aircraft to roll off the line in Des Moines in 2028, with full production ramping up to about 150 aircraft per year by the early 2030s.
The company evaluated more than a dozen sites for the facility, and chose the Seattle area for a simple reason: talent.

Harris cited the region’s robust aerospace legacy, as well as technology giants like Amazon and Microsoft and a burgeoning space and satellite industry which has taken shape in recent years. A number of fast-growing and heavily funded defense tech companies — including Anduril , Armada and Nominal — have also established beachheads in the region in recent years.
He described the X-BAT as a “modern sixth-generation fighter jet” that’s essentially a “flying sensor suite,” ingesting information in real time in order to make lightning-fast decisions.

Building that type of aircraft takes a very specialized workforce, one that Harris said is rooted across technology, aerospace, artificial intelligence, materials science and advanced manufacturing. Those are major strengths of the Seattle area workforce.

“We’re able to tap into that existing lineage and not have to necessarily train a workforce from the ground up, which would be hard to do on the timelines we’re trying to execute,” said Harris, who is planning to relocate to Washington state from Dallas.

To support its ambitious production schedule, Shield AI is actively recruiting across both software engineering and specialized aerospace roles. The initial hiring push for the Des Moines facility spans autonomy developers, flight-control software engineers, composite technicians, and shop-floor assembly specialists.

In one job listing for an engineering manager to lead the X-BAT hardware test software team, the company notes that the ideal candidate “has personally built or led the development of automated hardware test systems used in production, manufacturing, qualification, or other high-consequence environments.”

In another Seattle area job listing for a staff fuel engineer, the company says it is looking for a someone with “strong thermofluid fundamentals, engineering judgment, and the ability to understand fuel system behavior across demanding aircraft operating conditions while serving as the focal point between propulsion, vehicle teams, suppliers, and flight operations.”
Pay across those engineering roles ranges from $169,000 to $300,000 annually, according to the company job postings.

The company currently lists more than 110 open roles in the Seattle area, including a dozen or more in categories such as avionics and electrical; mechanical and thermal; software and networks; and aerostructures.
Choosing Washington also allowed Shield AI to buck a pervasive defense industry trend: separating engineering teams from physical factory floors to shave down labor costs.

While shifting assembly lines to lower-cost regions can cut costs, Harris said that remote manufacturing introduces hidden operational friction when building complex, software-defined aircraft like the X-BAT.

“We fundamentally believe in the colocation of engineering and production is the fastest way to bring capability to our customers,” said Harris, adding that combining engineering and production in a common facility is “one of the secret sauces of Shield.”
In a statement, U.S. Rep. Adam Smith (D-Wash.) — whose district includes Des Moines — welcomed Shield AI and the X-BAT manufacturing facility to King County.

“This hub will create high-quality jobs, strengthen Puget Sound’s expanding technology and aerospace sectors, and further diversify our local economy,” Smith said. “Reimagining aviation will have a rightful home here in Washington’s Ninth District.”
Katherine Caffrey, the city manager for City of Des Moines, welcomed the new jobs and economic investment in the community.

“Des Moines sits at the heart of the Puget Sound aerospace industry, and these jobs and this investment reflects exactly what we want Des Moines to be, a place where families can build strong careers close to home,” Caffrey said.

Shield AI officially introduced the X-BAT program to the public at an October 2025 event in Washington, D.C., unveiling the aircraft before an audience of military leaders, elected officials and defense industry partners.

At the time, Shield AI co-founder and president Brandon Tseng, a former Navy SEAL, called X-BAT a “transformative, runway-independent aircraft” and noted that “airpower without runways is the holy grail of deterrence.”

Last month, the U.S. Navy backed the program through an initial $50 million development contract , envisioning the autonomous fighter jets operating directly from destroyers, amphibious assault ships and converted cargo vessels to project long-range airpower without relying on traditional aircraft carriers.

That momentum grew internationally earlier this month, when Shield AI signed a five-year letter of intent with Polish defense companies PGZ and WZL-2. Under the framework, the companies are exploring plans to help build, supply, and repair the X-BAT, a partnership that could give NATO allies a fighter jet capable of operating even if local airfields and runways are destroyed or non-existent.

The X-BAT launches and lands vertically using a specialized Launch and Recovery Vehicle —a mobile trailer that erects the jet vertically, allowing it to be towed on interstate highways or loaded onto cargo ships to set up a field launch pad in minutes.

Harris noted that while a final site selection for manufacturing the LRV trailers has not been made, expanding production into the Puget Sound region remains on the table given the area’s deep manufacturing base.
In addition to the mammoth manufacturing facility in Des Moines, Shield AI announced that it is expanding its presence in both Texas and Kansas.

In Frisco, Texas, the company operates its X-Forge 1 site to handle core prototyping, software integration, and initial engineering for the autonomous fighter. Meanwhile, at X-Forge 2 in Newton, Kansas, Shield AI has expanded its airport footprint to serve as the program’s dedicated flight test, customer acceptance and maintenance hub.

Shield AI expects its X-Forge 2 site in Kansas to support approximately 1,800 regional jobs by the early 2030s, growing to 2,900 positions by 2046 with a projected $5 billion in regional economic impact over that period.

Addressing the cross-country logistics of moving completed aircraft from the Puget Sound assembly line to Kansas for flight testing, Harris explained that the X-BAT can be easily moved via the existing transportation corridors.
“The X-BAT is designed to be road transportable,” he said. “So we’re taking advantage of that.”
Beyond the immediate manufacturing logistics, Harris views the multi-billion-dollar expansion as a major long-term validation of the region’s industrial relevance .

articles.title: Kanu AI emerges from stealth with $11.7M to turn employee workflows into custom software
articles.author: John Cook
paras: Seattle-based Kanu AI announced $11.7 million in new funding on Wednesday to expand a platform that automatically turns everyday employee tasks into custom, enterprise-grade software.
Trilogy Equity Partners led the round, with participation from Andreessen Horowitz’s a16z speedrun, BMW i Ventures, and Accel.

Founded just over a year ago, Kanu AI addresses a common operational headache: valuable business knowledge getting trapped inside spreadsheets, inboxes, and individual workers’ heads. Rather than forcing companies to buy rigid off-the-shelf software or spend months on custom engineering, Kanu lets staff demonstrate how they complete work. The platform then builds, deploys, and updates those workflows directly within the customer’s cloud.

“Companies have spent decades buying software built around someone else’s idea of how they should work,” said Karan Grover, founder and CEO of Kanu AI. “Instead of renting generic intelligence from another vendor, companies can use Kanu to turn their own data, judgment, and operating expertise into an asset they own.”

Kanu reports that it has more than doubled its revenue in every quarter since launch. Its platform is currently used by enterprises across commercial real estate, insurance, financial services, and technology.

In one deployment for a national customer, Kanu said it compressed a complex data-analysis process spanning PDFs, emails, CRMs, and GIS systems from eight weeks down to under 10 minutes. The company expects the tool to cut its annual software costs by over $1 million while driving millions in new revenue.

To meet enterprise security standards, Kanu runs entirely inside the client’s own cloud infrastructure, ensuring data stays behind existing firewalls. The platform also includes human approval steps and provides full audit trails for every automated output.

Kanu AI plans to use the capital to hire across engineering and business roles. Its software is available today through the AWS and Google Cloud marketplaces. The company employs 10 people, with plans to reach about 15 employees by the end of the year.

Before founding Kanu AI, Grover was a machine learning engineer and three-time founder, as well as a Y Combinator alumnus. He previously worked as an engineer at Amazon and DoorDash. Early in his entrepreneurial career, he created a startup that built 3D audio tools to help blind individuals audibly “hear” and navigate their physical surroundings.

articles.title: City-backed cleaning crew offers proof of concept for Pike/Pine Business Improvement Area
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: The council president and the Pike/Pine clean-up crew (Image: @cmjoyhollings )
A city-funded street cleaning pilot across Pike/Pine is providing data and serving as a proof of concept for organizers working to establish a dedicated Business Improvement Area.

District 3 Councilmember Joy Hollingsworth praised the work of Seattle Surface Cleaners earlier this month, writing that the crew’s morning pressure washing and litter sweeps are an “investment focused on keeping Capitol Hill cleaner and improving the neighborhood.”

The pilot came about through a $300,000 citywide cleaning amendment sponsored last eyar by Councilmember Dan Strauss which allocated $100,000 each to Capitol Hill, Ballard, and the University District.

Alex Altshuler , Hollingsworth’s chief of staff, said that the cleaning funds are designed to work alongside a separate $50,000 budget addition intended to be complementary to the cleaning funds to “aid in the establishment of a BIA,” saying the program was structured as a “proof of concept” for corridor maintenance.

Because no formal BIA yet exists to collect ratepayer assessments, the interim funding is administered by the Seattle Office of Economic Development and fiscally sponsored by the University District Partnership .

Erin Fried of Hidden Cities Consulting , who manages the 15th Ave East BIA and is contracted by OED to guide the Pike/Pine effort, said the trial run is already “great for collecting data on what level of investment is truly needed.”

Over its first three months, the crew removed nearly 10,000 pounds of trash, scrubbed 4,420 graffiti tags, and handled 435 sanitary cleanups across a footprint running from Harvard Ave to 12th, including hot spots like the Neighbours Alley and walkways near Nagle Place next to Cal Anderson Park .
The baseline numbers arrive as organizers navigate the slow political process required to build a permanent assessment district.

As CHS reported in July , the campaign restructured after the GSBA chamber of commerce stepped back from organizing the zone, shifting OED’s direct collaboration to a stakeholder group of prominent local property owners, including Jill Cronauer of Hunters Capital, Liz Dunn of Dunn & Associates, and Don Blakeney of the Cal Anderson Park Alliance.
Hollingsworth has supported the Pike/Pine BIA effort as part of a multi-facet approach to improving public safety in the neighborhood.
A post shared by Seattle Surface Cleaners (@seattlesurfacecleaners)

Past efforts to form commercial districts on Capitol Hill have stumbled over boundary politics and assessment rates — most notably the bruising, failed push nearly a decade ago to expand the 1980s-era Broadway BIA Hill-wide, which contributed to the shutdown of the Capitol Hill Chamber of Commerce .

For the Pike/Pine BIA to move forward, organizers must translate the pilot’s workload metrics into a ratepayer business plan, define parcel borders, secure petition signatures from a majority of commercial property owners by assessed value, and shepherd the formation ordinance through the Seattle City Council.

But the path may be fluid. Earlier this month , the council approved an overhaul of the Broadway BIA’s outdated assessment structure in a boost that will greatly expand its current $200,000 a year budget. During the deliberations, Broadway BIA head Egan Orion told the council officials are exploring “a property-based model or establishing a brand-new BIA and sunsetting this particular model,” as property-based assessments “are more sustainable than B&O-based assessments.”
The Pike/Pine plan has been discussed as a property-based BIA.

Whether that Pike/Pine cleaning funds survive into 2027 will depend on the ongoing fall budget cycle as Mayor Katie Wilson tries to wipe out a $175 million deficit . Because the initial $100,000 cleaning allocation and $50,000 BIA startup grant were one-time council additions rather than permanent line items, Hollingsworth or other council allies will have to sponsor new amendments during the current balancing package deliberations, leaving the fate of continued city-backed cleaning dollars to be decided before final budget adoption in late November — or until property owners can finally agree on a self-funded district.

articles.title: 2027 minimum wage in Seattle will rise to $22.14
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: Seattle workers will see a bump in pay in 2027 as the city’s minimum wage climbs to $22.14 per hour effective January 1st, the Seattle Office of Labor Standards announced this week.

The upcoming adjustment represents an increase of 84 cents — roughly 3.9% — over the 2026 baseline rate of $21.30 per hour. As mandated by Seattle’s landmark 2014 Minimum Wage Ordinance, the yearly adjustments are pegged to regional inflation, calculated using the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers across the Seattle-Tacoma-Bellevue area.

The $22.14 standard applies equally across all employers regardless of company size. Following the 2025 sunset of the temporary tip-and-benefit credit once granted to small businesses, Seattle maintains a unified wage floor for large and small employers alike.
The annual setting of the inflation-pegged wage change more than a decade since Seattle established the “$15 Now” minimum wage in the city.
The movement began with calls for a $15 an hour minimum wage. It took Seattle seven years to get there.

Unanimously approved by the Seattle City Council in 2014, Chapter 14.19 required businesses in Seattle to incrementally raise their minimum wage each year until reaching $15 per hour over seven years. At the beginning of 2021, Seattle’s minimum wage increased to $16.69 per hour for large employers with more than 500 employees and small businesses with less than 500 employees finally reached the $15 an hour mark.
District 3 Councilmember Kshama Sawant held the minimum wage victory as the core accomplishment in her decade on the city council .

In 2024, efforts to roll back some of the $15 Now changes met with stiff opposition as current District 3 representative Joy Hollingsworth backed off a proposal to permanently extend a tip credit put in place ten years ago to protect the city’s small businesses during the phase-in of the higher minimum wage tied to inflation.
OLS said it will distribute updated workplace posters detailing the 2027 labor requirements in the coming weeks.

articles.title: Pinehurst Station Bursts into Action, as Upzones Trail Behind
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: Today, Pinehurst Station is officially a stop on both the 1 Line and 2 Line, bringing another Seattle neighborhood into the fold of the region's growing light rail system. Trains began stopping at Pinehurst bright and early at the start of service: 4:57am to be exact.
The Urbanist's Fall Member Drive is in final stretch! Support our work, read ad-free, and help us blow past our goal!

Pinehurst's opening day arrived five years sooner than the Sound Transit 3 (ST3) ballot measure pledged in 2016. The station's arrival and accelerated timeline is thanks to a concerted push from Seattle activists and leaders. Local organizer Renee Staton recounted that journey in a recent guest piece in The Urbanist .

The infill light rail station had been left on the cutting room floor as ST2 plans were formulated in 2008, but ST3 secured funding for the project with a 2031 opening targeted. Pinehurst ended up coming in at a cost of $240 million.

"Now, 2016, the region approved this station as part of Sound Transit 3, and we, at that time, operated 21 stations across 22 miles of track," Constantine said Tuesday. "Well, this station will be the 30th station we have opened since then. While almost tripling the track mileage, we'll now have 51 stations and 63 miles of track. That is a phenomenal pace of growth, and this is a system that our region has embraced wholeheartedly."

Sound Transit board members were convinced of the wisdom of opening the station shortly after the Lynnwood Link extension grand opening, voting to accelerate the timeline in 2020 and finalizing that decision a year later. Beyond simply wanting to deliver the station to North Seattle communities sooner, a practicality and cost-effectiveness argument swayed some votes. Construction costs tend to only climb with time, while fitting in construction windows becomes more difficult as ridership grows.

Lynnwood Link construction laid the track and the basic structure of the station, and some additional work happened before Lynnwood Link officially opened, though there were also significant disruptions to existing riders to get the station fully built after service commenced.

With the extension of the 2 Line across Lake Washington in March, regional light rail ridership has taken a big leap. Daily ridership exceeded 160,000 in April and continued to grow over the summer, spiking at a one-day record of 309,000 during Seattle's last World Cup match in July. This growth appears to have made Sound Transit the most-ridden light rail system in America – though several heavy rail metros have higher ridership.

The agency hosted a ribbon-cutting ceremony for its new infill station Tuesday afternoon, featuring a smorgasbord of speeches from local officials. Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson gave a nod to the leadership from transit advocates and Councilmember Debora Juarez (who wasn't in attendance) to make the station happen, and to the work ahead to make Graham Street infill station happen in Southeast Seattle.

"This is South Transit's first infill station, but it certainly will not be the last, and it happens because the people fought for it," Wilson said. "So thank you to Councilmember Juarez and all of the community advocates who made sure that Pinehurst did not get left behind. And thank you to the Sound Transit Board and agency for listening and delivering."

To the south in the Rainier Valley, Graham Street very nearly did not survive Sound Transit's "Enterprise Initiative" expansion plan overhaul in May. Board Chair Dave Somers proposed tabling the project indefinitely, but Wilson spearheaded a push to keep it on track to open around 2031. It ended up taking the pledge of $30 million in last-in funding from the City of Seattle to avoid the chopping block.

Located between Northgate and South Shoreline, Pinehurst Station is projected to attract 2,600 to 4,200 boardings daily boardings – at least once the system and surrounding neighborhood matures. That ridership would be on par with Mountlake Terrace (also near a golf course) and Beacon Hill. The late September opening coincides with the start of classes at the University of Washington and meets the agency's goal of opening the station in the third quarter of the year.

The station happened on a faster timeline than Seattle's rezoning process for the surrounding neighborhoods. The city had almost looked ready to advance its overdue Comprehensive Plan update until legal appeals derailed the process , forcing additional analysis on top of an environmental study that was already 1,300 pages long.

As a result, Pinehurst Station is surrounded by single family homes, a fenced-off City-owned golf course, and of course an obligatory gaping freeway trench spewing noise and pollution in the general vicinity. While the Comprehensive Plan declined to tackle the latter two issues, it had queued up rezones allowing five- to eight-story apartment buildings and ground-floor retail in several swaths of Pinehurst and some more limited areas of Haller Lake, replacing some broad areas of low-density Neighborhood Residential zoning.
Wilson acknowledged the delay and her resolve to see the rezones though, which she has also sought to augment with her Taller Faster Denser Plan .

"This is not just a station; it is a spark – a spark for long-term transformation in the newly designated Pinehurst-Haller Lake Urban Center, where we will see more homes, shops, services, parks, and walkable streets, all connected to great transit. That's what it's all about," Wilson said. "Sometimes we build transit where lots of density already exists, and sometimes we build transit, and we're able to welcome people around them."

Councilmember Dan Strauss – who like Wilson sits on the Sound Transit Board – upped the ante and declared Pinehurst a prime candidate for a freeway lid to create more developable land near the station and reconnect the street grid. As it stands, the west side of the station is cut off by I-5, with no safe bike facility and an unpleasant experience for those walking and rolling. Shoreline is building a pedestrian bridge at its 148th Street Station, but Seattle has no such facility planned.

"As we pass the Comprehensive Plan, there is more density. And when we are looking to reconnect across I-5, I talked today with Office of Planning and Community Development about the needing to lid I-5," Strauss said. "We can do so without any public funds. It recreates the grid. It increases the property tax that King County and Seattle has, and we had it done in Washington D.C. for zero public financing. This is a perfect candidate, and I'll tell you, it would not have the oomph if it weren't for this station."

Councilmember Eddie Lin, who chairs the land use committee, told the Seattle Times that he thinks it might be 2028 before the council is fully able to enact zoning changes, due to the need for additional time-consuming environmental studies to resolve the legal challenges.

While the Growth Management Hearings Board threw out the environmental complaints levied against Seattle's waylaid growth plan, it did find that the document failed to sufficiently study a higher growth scenario than the 120,000 new housing units over 20 years that was the upper echelon of Harrell's proposal. This is much to the chagrin of housing advocates who specifically pushed the Harrell administration to include a higher growth scenario in the plan. Over the last decade, Seattle has often exceeded the 6,000 homes per year production pace in the growth plan.

The upshot of this planning snafu is that Pinehurst likely waits a few more years for the blanket ban on new apartments to be lifted across much of its walkshed. At that point, perhaps an infusion of new housing will happen if interest from builders is there.

The Seattle Department of Transportation did deliver a number of street upgrades in time for the opening, including a new roundabout, protected bike lanes connecting Lake City to the station, new greenways, and a shared-use path to James Baldwin Elementary. The roundabout at Roosevelt and 125th is the first full-sized roundabout ever built inside city limits.

"About 90% of riders are expected to arrive without a car," Wilson said. "That is remarkable, and it's exactly why we have been investing in safer streets, new sidewalks, protected bike lanes, upgraded bus stops, and better buses. And for the real transportation wonks out there, we are excited to open the first roundabout in Seattle at Roosevelt Way NE and NE 125th Street."

King County Metro added Route 77 in its last service change providing a feeder route for the station that finally offers a direct bus connection between Lake City and Bitter Lake. Route 77 features 15-minute frequencies from 7am to 8pm, before dropping to half-hour headways thereafter. Other neighborhoods are feeling shortchanged by the adjustments Metro has been making around light rail openings, after losing direct connections that they once had.

Similar to other Sound Transit stations, artwork has been a major focus when it comes to potential placemaking. Pinehurst's prominent station art was designed by Seattle-based artist Romson Bustillo , who was born on the island of Mindanao in the Philippines. Human and animal figures brightly patterned in red, yellow, and green give the station a South Pacific vibe.

The station opening today will mark the last light rail opening in the region for quite some time. Sound Transit will roll out its Stride bus rapid transit network in 2028 and 2029. For light rail openings, Graham Street is next on deck in 2031. West Seattle Link has slipped to 2035 , which is also when Sound Transit is expecting to open Tacoma Dome Link . The agency is hoping to launch the first leg of the Everett Link extension (as far as Paine Field) in 2037.

Ballard Link, meanwhile, has considerable uncertainty, with 2042 for the whole line the best case scenario, which would require closing a huge budget gap of around $8 billion. The less-rosy scenario would be opening only the downtown portion in the 2040s and delaying the Interbay and Ballard section to the 2060s , pending enough funding accruing in Sound Transit coffers.

Another looming cloud on the horizon is labor strife. A half dozen picketers turned out to the ribbon-cutting with signs demanding a fair labor deal. One of those picketing Sound Transit workers, Brian Vierela, said a group currently exempt from collecting bargaining and working in project control, environmental permitting, community outreach, and systems engineering are seeking to unionize under Protec17, but they say they are being given the run around from a CEO that just got a lucrative extension himself .

"We're very happy that [Pinehurst] is opening," Vierela told The Urbanist . "We want to come here and show support for all of the workers that made this possible. But we're also very frustrated at the negotiating table with Dow. Recently Dow was able to have his contract renewed in about you know a handful of hours of the board deliberating. We have been at the negotiating table for over 18 months at this point, and we're here to essentially ask Dow to get us a deal and respect our union, and let's just move forward."
Ballard Congratulates Golf Course on Its New Light Rail Station: tinyurl.com/yncw9jep [image or embed]

The struggle to get light rail to Ballard while many less populous and popular destinations are added to the system led the satire site The Needling to write the headline "Ballard Congratulates Golf Course on Its New Light Rail Station."

While rezones bringing density are inbound eventually, for now the satirical headline isn't far off. Mike Lindblom's station opening preview in the Seattle Times wasn't much more sanguine, framing the station as a potential boondoggle. Lindblom noted that if the land use around the station isn't able to improve by leaps and bounds, ridership could skew toward the low end of Sound Transit's projections – with as few as 1,100 daily riders hopping on trains.
King County Councilmember Rod Dembowski took the opportunity to respond directly to those claims Tuesday.

"I know, Mr. Lindblom, that you know based on your reporting, there are some doubts about ridership, whether this should have been built, whether the investment was worth it," Dembowski said. "I'm here to tell you, we are here, and it was worth it. This station is going to deliver on riders. It's going to deliver on housing. It's going to deliver for Lake City that needed this investment, and I encourage everyone to do what I did: take the 77, a beautiful, brand new bus that adds east-west connections to this part of the city."

articles.title: Seattle as the Fourth Best Global City? Oxford Economics Says So
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: It was the best times; it was the worst of times. Depending whom you ask, Seattle's economy is one of the most elite in the world, or it's on death's doorsteps and in the midst of a corporate exodus . Oxford Economics weighed in this week on the positive side of the ledger, ranking Seattle as the fourth best city in the world on its 2026 Global Cities Index , trailing only New York, London and Paris.
The Urbanist's Fall Member Drive is in the home stretch! Support our work, read ad-free, and help us exceed our goal!

"Seattle’s economic strength propels it to the fourth spot of our 2026 Global Cities Index," the report noted. "This is largely thanks to the city’s major tech sector—home to both Microsoft and Amazon—which rivals those of any other city in the world. The metro also boasts major players in other industries such as aerospace (Boeing) and is home to major retail headquarters (Starbucks, Costco, and Nordstrom). This range of large employers gives the city one of the highest levels of GDP per person in our index and a healthy economic diversity measure."

The report was a good reminder that much is relative in economic analysis. Case in point: Mayor Katie Wilson's administration recently released a report that stressed that Seattle's economy (and the governmental revenue streams that rely on it) is not currently diversified enough, relying too heavily on a tech sector that could pull up stakes, or convert to an AI robot workforce that leaves many locals out of a job. Wilson launched a Resilient Seattle Economy Task Force to work on the issue and craft a strategy to grow and diversify the local economy.

At a recent public appearance , Wilson noted it is tough to manage the tension of wanting to decrease income inequality and rein in big tech's power while not killing the golden goose that is paying a big chunk of the City of Seattle's bills. The campaign that swept Wilson into office was focused on affordability and the idea that Seattle's economic boom should be more broadly shared. That campaign touched on improving governance, quality life, and environmental stewardship.

While the global index seems geared toward indicating business opportunities to corporate leaders, Oxford Economics – a commercial advisory firm based in Oxford, England – notes the analysis goes beyond solely looking at economic output: "We score cities based on a range of metrics across five categories: Economics, Human Capital, Quality of Life, Environment, and Governance."

Oxford's authors pointed out that very high incomes can be a double-edged sword contributing to climbing housing prices, especially as housing supply lags – with Seattle's slow pace to easing zoning restrictions and other development hurdles partially to blame for that lag.

"The city scores favourably in the Quality of Life category as a concentration of high-value sectors results in Seattle residents having a very high income per person (fourth in the world). However, this can be a double-edged sword, as income inequality is also considerably high in the city. This is especially concerning as Seattle’s consistent population growth and limited housing supply are set to contribute to increasingly unaffordable house prices and rents."
Seattle had the second highest quality of life ranking in the United States (22nd globally), behind San Jose, California, which (perhaps bizarrely) ranked 13th in the globe.

Seattle's qualify of life was on full display on the international stage this summer as the city's downtown hosted six FIFA Men's World Cup matches and earned the city a distinction as a top host with a booming transit system , bustling pedestrian zone, and beautiful waterfront park. The Bay Area, meanwhile, trucked fans to distant Santa Clara to watch matches in suburban recluse mode. How's that for quality of life?

Seattle also generally outperforms the U.S. field when it comes to environmental footprint and climate pollution per capita , with a big credit going to policies limiting suburban sprawl and promoting housing growth in transit-rich areas. Plus, with perhaps the most ambitious transit expansion plans in the country, the Seattle metropolitan area is adding more transit-rich areas – albeit with some snags and delays along the way .

While Oxford Economics top 100 list is heavily weighted toward the Anglo world and Europe, authors do note that Asia is seeing some of fastest economic growth and is climbing the ranks. While pure GDP per capita (on which Seattle ranks 4th in the world at $152,000) seems the largest weight in the index, some cities climb the rankings due to quality of life, governance, and environmental factors, with European standouts often taking that route.

"Cities across North America and Europe dominate the top reaches of our index, with the US alone accounting for 30 of the top 100 cities," the report states. "Yet the drivers of this dominance between the two regions differs. In the US, it is strong scores across the Economics and Human Capital categories that drive their elevated position. In Europe, however, it is outperformance across the Quality of Life, Environmental, and Governance categories. These differences are emblematic of current trends and policy priorities, as the US continues to post strong economic gains, while Europe retains its advantage in resident amenities and liveability."

Another trend the report highlights is how Trump's erratic policymaking impacts the governance of American cities and the how its anti-immigrant policies could starve American cities of their lifeblood of talented immigrants that propel their economic engines. The authors ranked all U.S. cities 198th on governance, a swipe at the Trump administration, and they highlighted the threat that Trumpism posed to Seattle in particular.

"[T]he downside risk of the Trump administration’s immigration policies will likely limit international immigration to the city, reducing population growth and the share of foreign-born residents," the report said. "This may hold Seattle back from making gains in the Human Capital category in the next few years."

Beyond federal chaos, part of Seattle's governance challenge is high mayoral turnover. Wilson will likely seek to break the run of one-term mayors, but several members of the local mainstream media appear to have already turned against her, concocting negative headlines to the detriment of more positive stories that are out there, as this recent Oxford Economics report illustrates.

articles.title: 40 Acre Conservation League seeks to protect land for future generations
articles.author: Alison Mariella Désir
paras: As you may know, I have a podcast called Earthmovers that features conversations with trailblazers who are reclaiming the narrative in their respective spaces of influence. I recently had the opportunity to speak with Jade Stevens , cofounder of the 40 Acre Conservation League , California’s first Black-led land conservancy. Jade is a POWERHOUSE and somebody who gives me faith in our future.

The name of the conservancy pays homage to a broken promise made to formerly enslaved African Americans after the Civil War, who were promised forty acres and a mule to provide a modicum of reparations for what they had endured and to restart a life in the newly reformed country.

Jade’s organization carries the torch, with the vision of both protecting land for generations to come and providing public access to the land for recreation for generations to come. At a time when the current administration is reducing public lands and hobbling the Endangered Species Act, knowing that people like Jade exist and are doing the important work of conserving essential resources for future generations is a literal breath of fresh air.

Part of Jade’s work is also to reconnect Black people with our ancestral relationship to the land. While Black people have faced and continue to face prejudice and hatred in the outdoors in the United States, many Black people in this country descend from enslaved Africans who were kidnapped and stolen from Africa specifically for their expertise in land stewardship and farming. Being connected to the land is not new to us – it is in fact a return and a reclamation.
I can’t stop thinking about her important work and I encourage you to learn more about it!

It is officially mushroom foraging season! I have plans on the calendar to go matsutake mushroom foraging and I’m reminded of season 3, episode 5 when I had the opportunity to go foraging with PeiPei Sung, a mycology enthusiast. What I have found is that having hobbies and interests throughout the rainy and dark season here in Seattle makes life more bearable. Rather than dreading the darkness, I can look forward to what this season makes possible.

articles.author: Jaelynn Grisso
paras: VHS and other magnetic media empowered people to record everything - from public spectacles to home life. But the tape and media are degrading, and archivists are sounding the alarm that history will be lost if they aren’t saved.
MIPoPS, or Moving Image Preservation of Puget Sound, works with a range of organizations in the region to preserve their magnetic media, such as VHS or audio cassettes.

Magnetic media degrades more quickly than other media types like film. For example, a standard VHS tape only lasts for 10 to 30 years. That’s why the Library of Congress estimates most magnetic media will need to be digitized and archived by 2032.
Acting executive director Libby Hopfauf said it’s also important to preserve this media specifically because of the role it played in giving more widespread access to recording.

“Film was really expensive for a while,” Hopfauf said. “So, really, only people who had money could afford to buy equipment and record their own stories. Then when video was introduced, a lot more people were able to purchase the equipment and all of their tapes that they had. It was also more portable, so it's easier to carry around and tell your own story. And that's just really important because a lot of communities who didn't really have a voice and recorded history, like in moving image recordings, were able to document their stories and their cultures and their experience.”
MIPoPS has already digitized more than 12,000 tapes, but Hopfauf says there are thousands more to go before the 2032 deadline.

“Since magnetic media is actively dying, there's a lot of urgency around that to help support those preservation efforts before time runs out, and then important, unique content is lost forever,” she said.
By Venice Buhain , story published 09/29/2026
What launched more than 20 years ago as the annual Tasveer South Asian Film Festival now has a permanent home with the aim to build community.

Tasveer bought the century-old building in Seattle’s Columbia City neighborhood in 2025, after the beloved Ark Lodge Theater closed after 12 years in operation. The $3 million building was purchased with the help of a grant from 4Culture, which manages the county’s lodging and arts tax revenue.
“It was a 15 year long dream that we harbored to have our own space and create our own, art space and do our own events,” Tasveer co-founder and executive director Rita Meher said.
Meher co-founded the Tasveer South Asian Film Festival to focus on South Asian stories in the aftermath of 9/11.

“We saw there was a lot of hate and xenophobia, homophobia, Islamophobia in everywhere. Even I was I experienced some hate incident in Seattle, which is hard to believe. So that moment kind of changed me. And when my friend said, we should do something and start an organization to create a dialog around important social justice topics, I jumped on an idea,” Meher said.
Meher thought that film was an ideal medium to build a platform.
“You don't have to always understand the language,” she said. “An image can speak thousand words and it permeates deeper and widely very quickly.”
"No offense to books, but reading a book... you do it so single, sitting by yourself, but watching a film you can watch with the whole community and talk about it,” she said.

In the two decades since Tasveer was founded, the small organization has grown its impact. It is the only Oscar-qualifying South Asian film festival, and gets represented at major film festivals, including Sundance and the Toronto International Film Festival. But its core mission has remained largely the same.
“The original mission to inspire social change to film arts and storytelling,” Meher said. “That baseline is always there. But how we do it and how we adhere to that mission always evolve with time.”
The big change with the new building is that the organization is more accessible and can provide more opportunities for all of Seattle’s communities.

“Even though we are we started out to serve South Asian community, we are serving wider community that needs our space, our platform and tell their stories. And and we need also our community's help to help us stay in business and continue on. And yeah, it's a great place to come watch an independent film,” Meher said.
The 2026 Tasveer South Asian Film Festival runs October 13 through 18 at the Tasveer Film Center at 4816 Rainier Ave. S. in Seattle’s Columbia City neighborhood.
By Taylor Mirfendereski , story published 09/30/2026
Most sticky notes don’t survive the week. They hold a grocery list or a phone number and then end up in the trash.
Clare Johnson has kept hers for more than two decades.

Every night before bed, the Seattle artist draws one moment from her day on a 3-by-3-inch Post-it and adds a few words. It might be a swim with her dad, a friend’s joke, a bad migraine or a deeper thought.
“I thought it would be amazing to document my life in something that was meant to be thrown away — that was disposable,” Johnson, 45, said. “Instead of throwing them away, I save them forever.”

She calls the project “A Life in Sticky Notes.” The collection now contains more than 6,700 notes, a record of most of her adult life. This spring Johnson’s collection filled a Pioneer Square gallery . Now, she’s sharing the project in talks across the state through Humanities Washington’s Speakers Bureau , where she encourages audiences to hold on to small moments and create daily rituals of their own.

“It’s really a memoir, but a visual memoir … one that happens in real time, one night at a time,” Johnson said. “It gives me this great joy to complete a little art project at the end of the day and communicate something that I’m excited to share or to remember for myself.”

The big moments of her life are in the collection — her divorce, health problems and a move across the ocean — but they’re not what stand out among the thousands of notes. Many of the notes save the smallest moments that got her through the hard years.
“I won’t necessarily forget that my mom had cancer at a certain time … but I might forget this really delightful interaction that I had with a stranger,” Johnson said.
Johnson started the project in 2005 as a 23-year-old graduate art student in London. The idea began with grief.
After a close friend died suddenly, Johnson, who paints and does ink drawings, said she found herself unable to make anything. What finally got her working again was a pack of sticky notes.

“Making those little paintings on Post-it notes felt almost like me tricking myself into feeling like art was approachable again by using this really small format,” she said. “I really like that intimate square, small size. It’s very ordinary.”
The ritual that grew from it has helped her in other ways, too.

Johnson is neurodivergent and has a condition called visual snow syndrome, which fills her vision with tiny flashing dots, even with her eyes closed. Bedtime has been a struggle since she was a child.
Drawing before sleep gave her “some distraction, some safety,” she said.
“It’s both an art project and a very personal ritual that I designed for myself and my own brain and my own needs,” she said.
“I needed a way to both hold memories and make my life feel visible as a queer person, whose history has been actively erased,” she said.

When Johnson’s exhibition opened in May, strangers found pieces of themselves in it. One woman emailed her about a sticky note that simply says “clean sheets!” It made the woman think about changing her sheets more often, Johnson said.

“This project shows how many little tiny things are inside each person that we would never know about and maybe still can’t even understand,” she said. “Little moments have the power to be wonderful, even when other things are difficult.”

articles.title: Pop Loser: Where Are They Now? (Albino Burmese Python Edition)
articles.author: Audrey Vann
paras: Welcome back to Pop Loser! Spiritually, I’m in a place of the 2001 VMAs when Britney Spears debuted “I’m a Slave 4 U,” and apparently I’m not alone—the track is having a moment with Gen Z. I’ll dive into some herstory about the albino Burmese python from the famed VMAs performance. Plus, the 2026 VMAs happened this weekend, if you even care. And oh my god, Tinashe’s new album Popstar is perfect.
This week in Strangerland, I attended Lily Allen’s West End Girl tour at the Paramount on Thursday night, which was a masterclass in public shaming. Read my full review here.

On Friday, the Space Needle glowed pink in honor of Dolly Parton. The occasion marked Seattle’s first official Dolly Day, 9/25 (a reference to 9 to 5 ), which councilmember Alexis Mercedes Rinck announced last week. The Pacific Science Center, Lumen Field, the Great Wheel, and Columbia Tower also added touches of pink to the skyline in Parton’s honor.

Spiritually, I’m in a place of the 2001 VMAs, when Britney Spears debuted “I’m a Slave 4 U,” adorned in body glitter and dripping with sweat, with an albino Burmese python draped around her neck. And I’m not alone—according to Rolling Stone , new Spotify data shows that the 25-year-old song is trending amongst Gen Z. Fifty-five percent of global streams in the past month came from listeners born between 1997 and 2012. Twenty-seven percent of listeners were not even born when Spears debuted the song.

Fun fact: The celebrated serpent featured in the VMAs performance is apparently named “Banana,” something I learned back in 2006 when she was used in a photo shoot on America’s Next Top Model . MTV staff writer Crystal Bell tracked the python down in 2016 to confirm that the female snake was still alive and had, in fact, grown nearly four times larger; the owners estimated she weighed in at around 20 pounds in 2001 and had grown to roughly 100 pounds (and around 14 feet long). Personally, I need to see another 10-year update on Banana.

Speaking of the VMAs, that happened over the weekend (if you even care). Madonna opened the show (her first VMA performance in 23 years) with Sabrina Carpenter and Charli XCX (nobody kissed , unfortunately). There were also cameos from Julia Garner, Seth Rogen, Andrew Watt, Debi Mazar, Gabbriette, SOMBR, and Madonna’s ex, Tony Ward (who appears in music videos for “Cherish,” “Justify My Love,” and “Erotica”).

Other highlights from the 2026 VMAs included two very unrehearsed speeches from Madonna, who won Best Collaboration and Best Dance (and several other untelevised categories). When the Queen of Pop accepted the award for Best Dance, she feigned pulling a laser out of her ass, then remarked: “I’m kind of unclear what this award is for…” (It was for “Confessions II.”)

Oh, you wanted some highlights that didn’t include Madonna? Fine. Kacey Musgraves performed a beautiful tribute to Dolly Parton, singing “I Will Always Love You” while sheathed in a Dolly-style, sequin-crusted pink gown trimmed in ostrich feathers. Snoop Dogg hosted the event and delivered a dozen jokes that didn’t make any sense, at one point telling a knock-knock joke with a “deez nuts” punchline. SOMBR, Raye, Teddy Swims, and Adam Lambert paid tribute to the late George Michael, and it’s best I don’t say anything more about that…

When SZA met Danny. SZA was inducted into the New Jersey Hall of Fame on Friday, but “more importantly,” as she put it, she was able to meet fellow inductee Danny DeVito, who also hosted the ceremony. The meeting is evidenced by two adorable photos—a selfie and a photo of them taking the selfie. DeVito is sporting a suit, paired with black Crocs. Stars—they’re just like us!

articles.title: Slog AM: Some in Seattle Felt that Earthquake, Repeal of Washington’s Millionaires Tax Is Polling Poorly, Sen. Amy Klobuchar Saves the Day
articles.author: Charles Mudede
paras: Seattle just can’t stop dying. The 2026 Global Cities Index by Oxford Economics clearly shows it has one foot in the grave. How else to explain the city being rated fourth in the whole fucking world when it comes to “economics, human capital, quality of life, environment, and governance.” What a catastrophe . Seattle is only behind Paris, London, and Mamdaniland. You got that right. The 206 beat big time players like San Francisco, Tokyo, Berlin, and Toronto. Why? Because of its exceptional concentration of “human capital,” which, in 2025, resulted in a metropolis with an impressive $632 billion GDP. Now think about this for a moment. That’s not far from Shanghai’s GDP ($816 billion). But that financial center has a population of 24 million. Our metropolitan area is just 4.1 million. Seattle, death becomes you.

Clearly, what our city needs is not more capitalism, we are filled to the gills with all of that stuff. What we really need is more socialism. We are way behind in that department. But when, say, Mayor Katie Wilson proposes expanding Seattle transit she must resort to a sales tax increase. What’s sad in all of this is the city, a super-rich city, can’t find any other way to fund something that’s so vital to its general well-being. In our town, there’s only money for making more money (M-M) and no money for making life livable for those whose “human capital” does not make the cash registers sing.

A quick note. The concept of “human capital” has an origin. It’s a 1964 book, Human Capital: A Theoretical and Empirical Analysis by Gary Becker, an economist who was part of the Chicago School of Economics. In short, he was a neoliberal. And the true (and even nefarious) goal of his human capital project was to convince wage earners (store attendants, mechanics, janitors, plumbers, bus drivers, you name it), that they were just like their exploiters: capitalists. A wage, in this view of things, was a return on your capital. And going to school was like a speculator investing in a new luxury tower. Even crossing the border sans-papiers was an investment on your capital. For this neoliberal nonsense, which was popularized in 2005 by the mind-numbingly dumb book Freakoconomics , Becker received a Nobel prize in economics in 1992.

A new statewide poll shows that the initiative to repeal Washington’s Millionaires Tax is in trouble. Seattle Times reports that 57 percent of voters rejected Initiative 645 when its fiscal hit on the state’s budget (cuts in healthcare and education) was explained, as opposed to 35 percent who, nevertheless, gave it a thumbs up. The supporters of the repeal of course do not want voters to know about this impact; they are desperate to keep the consequences in the dark. But that’s not going to happen. The needed fiscal information will appear on the ballot in November.

Did you feel that? I didn’t. The earthquake that happened near Port Orchard around 2:05 p.m. yesterday . I completely missed it. Though some claim they felt the ground move a little beneath their feet. So far, no damage to life and property has been reported.

Yesterday was perfect. Low and slow-moving clouds. Rain now and then. Leaves swirling in the wind. Wheeling birds above the trees. Lovers kissing on a wet sidewalk. Dogs in raincoats. Highs below 60. An early dusk. A longish night. A dream about a long-dead and mostly forgotten foe. Today will not be as nice. Dark clouds will not carry the sun away. Expect a high of 64.

Astronomers at the Roque de los Muchachos Astrophysical Observatory have identified the “ largest known galaxy .” Its name: IC 1101. Its distance from us: 1.7 million light-years. Its size: “wider than 17 Milky Ways lined up in a row.” Does that make you feel so small? Insignificant like a speck of dust? As trivial as a puff of smoke? If so, it would do you well to recall this line by America’s greatest poet, Emily Dickinson : “The Brain — is wider than the Sky — For — put them side by side — The one the other will contain / With ease — and You — beside —”

There is no doubt in my mind that Sen. Eric Schmitt knew exactly what he was doing, when, during a bogus Senate Judiciary Committee hearing concerning the investigation that followed Trump’s attempted coup on January 6, 2021, he asked the former special counsel Jack Smith if he attended an Atlanta Hawks game on February 3, 2024. Of course Smith said no; and of course Schmitt unrolled with the fervor and quickness of an ejaculating demon some conspiracy theory concerning an encounter with Fani Willis, the Black district attorney of Fulton County, Georgia. (Both rightly went after Trump for breaking the law.) Schmitt claimed he had text messages from Smith’s team that proved he went to the game, accused him of perjury, went on about the Soviet Union, and finally called him a “total dirtbag.” And that was the whole point. Schmitt had nothing more to say. He wanted to move on. He put suspicion in the air. Mainstream media would take care of the rest: Smith Met Willis During a Hawks Game? And it would likely stick, despite the lack of evidence. But then came the surprise and what must be one of the most comic moments in the history of Senate hearings.

Thanks to the tenacity of Sen. Amy Klobuchar it was eventually revealed that Jack Smith had been to a basketball game on February 3 , but it was in Maryland, and involved the Iowa Hawkeyes, a college women’s basketball team, not the Atlanta Hawks, a professional men’s team. The conspiracy theory died almost as soon as it was born. And what the dodo senator from the Show-Me State, Schmitt, exposed instead was yet another great waste of taxpayers’ money. This hearing, that ballroom, the helipad, Trump’s tax-funded political ad, and so on and so on. What we see day after day is the brazen blazing of public cash.

Ain’t that America. Arkansas’ governor, Sarah Huckabee Sanders, made an ad that said the usual kind of right-wing crap: people don’t work because they are too lazy, and so welfare is just a waste of taxpayers’ money. But here is the thing: her example of a lazy welfare recipient was a young white male eating snacks and playing video games in a dark room. This depiction apparently upset her base because it was further evidence of the persecution of white males in our society. They have it so, so bad. And this ad only made matters worse. It would have been better, and more accurate, if Sanders showed black males with their pants sagging or black women with too many babies. A comment on X: “Our government has systematically discriminated against white males for decades now, and yet now has the audacity to dishonestly mock young white males as welfare queens.” Even if it’s true, which it’s not, you are still talking about decades? What about 400 years of slavery? In the words of Burning Spear: “Do you remember the days of slavery. How they worked us so hard.”
In fact, let’s end AM with Burning Spear’s Slavery Days .

articles.title: Antarctica’s ice loss is locked in, and extra snowfall won’t save it – that’s bad news for low-lying coastal areas elsewhere
articles.author:
<name>Yucheng Lin, Assistant Professor of Energy and Environment, City University of Hong Kong</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/yucheng-lin-2767294"/>
paras: Sea-level rise is one of the most visible signs of climate change, one that is threatening low-lying coastal communities around the world. Today, about 1 billion people live in coastal areas; about 100 million live within 1 meter (3.3 feet) of sea level, highly exposed to coastal flooding.
Over the long term, when it comes to future sea-level rise, one place matters more than any other: Antarctica.

The frozen continent holds enough ice to raise global sea level by about 190 feet (58 meters) . Yet scientists have disagreed on a fundamental question: Will Antarctica gain more ice than it loses this century or lose more ice than it gains?
In a new study published in the scientific journal Nature Geoscience , we looked at hundreds of thousands of potential futures and the impact of each on the ice sheet.

We found that Antarctica’s ice loss this century is locked in – even if the world limits global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit), the 2015 international Paris climate agreement’s most ambitious goal.
The Antarctic ice sheet’s future depends on a chain of events.

Greenhouse gas emissions from vehicles, coal- and natural gas-fueled power plants and other sources around the world determine how much the ocean and air around Antarctica warms. That warming shapes how ice shelves around the continent’s margins melt, and how quickly the glaciers behind them slide over the bedrock. When those ice shelves thin or collapse, studies show the glacier flow speeds up .

Each step relies on assumptions that scientists have yet to agree on, such as how ice shelves collapse . Different assumptions give different answers, and because each step feeds the next, the differences grow – what scientists call cascading uncertainty. As a result, research teams around the world can’t agree on whether Antarctica will gain or lose ice this century.

Snow is part of the puzzle. Warmer air holds more moisture, so as temperatures rise, more snow will likely fall on Antarctica . In some projections, that extra snow outweighs the ice lost to the warming ocean, and the ice sheet actually grows.
A big reason for this persistent disagreement involves the cost of computing.

Each ice-sheet simulation runs with just one set of assumptions for every step in the chain, from how much greenhouse gas we emit to how the ice behaves. One run can keep a supercomputer busy for days, so no team can test every plausible combination.

Our team of data scientists, glaciologists and oceanographers took a shortcut. An international project called the Ice Sheet Model Intercomparison Project, or ISMIP6 , has built a large archive of Antarctic simulations showing how the ice responds under different circumstances. We trained a physics-informed machine learning model on that archive to learn how each simulation’s outcome depends on its physical assumptions, such as how easily ice slides over bedrock. The machine learning model does in a fraction of a second what took the original models days, predicting sea-level change with similar accuracy.

That speed let us run millions of combinations and check hundreds of thousands of possible futures against data from satellites that weigh the ice sheet from space by sensing tiny changes in Earth’s gravity. Only scenarios that were able to match what the satellites have seen since 2002 made the cut.
The scenarios that did make the cut point one direction: Antarctica will lose more ice than it gains this century , even if humanity is able to limit global warming to 1.5 C .

That means Antarctica will contribute more to sea-level rise that’s already being driven by melting of the Greenland ice sheet and mountain glaciers and from warming ocean temperatures that cause water to expand.

The biggest lessons from our study are that greenhouse gas emissions matter and extra snowfall won’t save Antarctica . Every ton of greenhouse gas that humans can avoid releasing today reduces how much ice Antarctica loses this century, and the benefit – slower and less sea-level rise – lasts for hundreds of years.

In a scenario with very high emissions, our results show a potential faster domino effect. A fast-warming ocean thins the ice shelves, weakened shelves break apart, and glacier ice flows into the ocean faster. Each step makes the next one easier. Together, these steps could add up to 10 inches (25 centimeters) of sea-level rise from Antarctica alone by 2100 – enough to permanently flood the homes of more than 10 million people .

Of more than 20 physical assumptions about Antarctica, three matter most for understanding future sea-level rise: how ice shelves respond to a warming ocean, how ice slides over bedrock , and how fast the ocean and air around Antarctica warm . Gaining a better understanding of these processes would do the most to sharpen sea-level projections.

Some processes are missing from today’s simulations, so our machine learning model can’t learn about them – for example, how ice cracks and breaks , and how rivers and lakes beneath the ice sheet change over time. Any of these could change our understanding of how quickly Antarctica’s ice reaches the sea and whether coastal communities have enough time to adapt.

What our study does offer is a much faster way to test combinations of assumptions that are too costly to simulate one by one. That provides a clearer basis for the decisions coastal communities around the world are already having to make.
