The financial issues creeping up on SDOT are impacting the transportation fund, the primary source of transportation funding outside of the $1.55 billion, eight-year transportation levy voters approved in 2024 . According to a presentation made to the Seattle City Council's budget committee Monday, SDOT would have been looking at a $113 million deficit in the transportation fund by 2028 without any adjustments.

"Our costs have continued to rise while revenues have flattened or declined, resulting in recent budget appropriations outpacing available resources and driving down our fund balances," Kris Castleman, SDOT's Director of Finance & Administration, told councilmembers Monday. "We are at a critical financial inflection point, and targeted intervention is needed now to balance the budget, maintain cash to fund our daily operations, and safeguard our future with a path toward long-term financial stability."

These adjustments to SDOT's budget come as part of Mayor Katie Wilson's $9.1 billion draft budget , unveiled last week. The new mayor's first budget, the package has drawn attention for being more focused on setting the city on a sustainable path , putting the days of continued projected deficits in out years behind it after heavy usage under former Mayor Bruce Harrell.

Changes to SDOT's budget already made in 2026 include $56.7 million in reductions, including nearly $14 million in program cuts. Milder winter weather earlier this year allowed the department's emergency services budget to be cut by 56%, and planned maintenance work on the city's traffic signals were moved to 2027, resulting in a 39% cut in that program. But reductions in future years will be more painful, and include cuts to pothole repair and major bridge maintenance projects.

With a reduction in pothole repair funding, SDOT expects to slip closer to its voter-approved target of filling 80% of reported potholes within 72 hours, compared to its nearly 90% rate reported currently. Major repaving work on city arterial streets will rebound to historic levels, despite a boost in maintenance funding from the Seattle Transportation Levy put forward by Harrell and expanded by Council.

2026 adjustments have also included the "abandonment" of years of capital funds that had been carried forward from prior years but didn't get utilized. The practice of carrying funds forward from the prior year after the department wasn't able to spend all of its budget has been one that has been ongoing for years, and has often made it hard to truly understand the department's financial outlook.

The proposed cuts will have some staffing impacts. Out of 1,291 total full-time positions at SDOT, nine positions that are currently unfilled will be permanently eliminated, including three civic engineer positions, three signal electricians, two maintenance laborers, and one traffic sign and signal crew chief. But the department's staff capacity will be largely insulated from cuts – at least for now.

Also insulated from cuts are traffic safety programs, with Acting SDOT Director Angela Brady telling councilmembers that the Vision Zero budget for 2026-2028 is actually set to increase by $1 million across the three years. However, many more projects than just the ones in the Vision Zero program impact safety, and even reductions in the pothole program can impact safety for people who walk and roll on Seattle's streets.

"I want to be clear that street safety and Vision Zero, as a program, remain fully funded in this budget," Brady said. "We know how important this program is to Seattle citizens, our mayor, and our councilmembers."

Wilson, in her budget speech last week , also called out transit speed and reliability investments as an area where focus will be maintained, in the wake of the successful implementation of a long-envisioned bus lane on Denny Way for the Route 8. That $5 million project was funded by the 2024 transportation levy.
Additional funds for bus upgrades are included in Wilson's renewal of the Seattle Transit Measure, on the ballot in November.
While more streets are being eyed for bus lanes, those projects aren't moving forward with the alacrity of the mayoral-directed Denny Way project.
Such a dramatic adjustment to scale back programs will absolutely have an impact on the ability for Wilson – and for city councilmembers – to get new projects added to SDOT's workplan.

"We also want to note that today's updates about reductions, limited reserves, and uncertain funding make our overall position to handle new requests less flexible," Castleman said. "New priorities, projects, programs, and policies that are unfunded can present a zero-sum game in this financial environment. So, as we engage with communities, businesses and our elected leadership, folks are likely to hear even more from SDOT about trade-offs."
During Monday's meeting, a question from Councilmember Dionne Foster probed into the issues with the transportation fund, and how this issue has popped up seemingly out of nowhere.

"With the transportation fund, this has been building for several years," City Budget Director Aly Pennucci said. "As a city, we have been hyperfocused on the general fund deficit, and there's been less public conversation about the projected deficit in the transportation fund that was not ideal, but was present in the financial plan that was part of the adopted budget last year, and then the combination of actual expenses, actual revenues, and the automatic carry forward in the capital budget kind of all came to a head."

Wilson's proposed budget for SDOT does pull a few levers in hopes of improving the department's financial picture. It increases the city's Commercial Parking Tax rate from 14.5% to 17%, a move that brings in nearly $10 million per year that will go to both Vision Zero and programs like sign maintenance and urban forestry that would otherwise see steeper cuts.

Traffic enforcement cameras are also expected to be a budget lifeline, with an additional $20 million per year by 2028 expected following the expansion of the speed camera program beyond time-limited school zones next year. Pennucci told councilmembers that those projections are conservative, given the fact that SDOT has not yet implemented 24/7 speed cameras on any arterial corridors.

A new 0.1% countywide sales tax for county roads will also benefit SDOT, thanks to a forthcoming pass-through program intended to fund local transportation needs. In June, when the creation of that program was being debated, it nearly included a provision that would have capped Seattle's contributions as the largest city in the county, but that cap was removed after pushing by city leaders and advocates. As a result, $4.7 million a year is set to prevent cuts to SDOT's urban forestry program and some bridge maintenance work.

At Monday's initial discussion of SDOT's budget, councilmembers raised concerns around projects in their districts potentially getting shortchanged, including a lack of ongoing funding for the council-created District Project Fund . A proposal that was spearheaded by transportation chair Rob Saka, that fund provided $7 million in 2025 and 2026 for hand-picked transportation projects in each of the seven council districts, but no ongoing funding for that fund had been identified beyond this year. If the District Project Fund is to continue, it will fall on the council to decide what other line items should be cut from the department's budget.
The hope is that by overhauling SDOT's budget and "right-sizing" program budgets to align with available resources, the department can be put on more stable footing.

"What is especially urgent for us is that our flexible funding sources are becoming even more tightly constrained, and yet they are used for core services and help us to be responsive to emerging needs from both our elected officials and the community," Castleman said. "We're also addressing the very real need to create financial stability for the department."
The Seattle City Council will hold a public hearing on Wilson's draft budget next Tuesday, October 5 , at 1 pm and 5 pm.

articles.title: Katie Wilson’s City-Centered Anti-Fascist Playbook Emerges at Author Talk
articles.author: Amy Sundberg
paras: Last week, Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor made an appearance at Seattle Town Hall in conversation with Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson to promote their new book, End Times Fascism , which has become an international bestseller .

Both the book and a 10-minute video shown at the beginning of the talk open with the story of a presentation by American real estate moguls Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff at the annual summit of the World Economic Forum in Davos this past January. The two men shared their vision for redeveloping Gaza into a resort city for the super-rich, a flagship project for President Donald Trump’s “Board of Peace.”
“Let’s just plan for catastrophic success,” Kushner said at the event.
End Times Fascism posits that while there is much to learn from looking at the history of fascism, the path of fascism today is precipitated by different crises than those in the past.
“We think of fascism as capitalism's most ferocious threat response,” Klein said. “It emerges during times of crisis, when the system is collapsing and failing people on a mass scale.”

However, the details around how it emerges and functions can differ. We live in a world of advanced technologies compared to, say, post-World War I Germany – including nuclear weapons and comprehensive surveillance – and we are confronting an accelerating climate crisis in the wake of the trauma caused by the global Covid-19 pandemic.

These different crises, the authors argue, have led to changes in the far-right and shaped the alliance of forces pushing fascism in this and other countries: an alliance bound by their fascination with the idea of a forthcoming apocalypse. In the book, the authors detail the three main groups as they see them, all of whom agree in pushing the idea of the world being in its end times: the religious extremists, the tech oligarchs, and the ethno-nationalists.

“We argue in the book that fascism, in addition to being a response to systemic crises, is also a response to these credible threats from the left,” Taylor said. In the past, those credible threats included events like the Russian Revolution and the beginning of the Reconstruction after the American civil war. In the most recent fascist push, Taylor said those threats have included Black Lives Matter, the Me Too movement, and the revitalization of labor unions.

The book concludes by building the case for a movement dedicated to “hereness.” Unlike the fascist trio of groups detailed above, who believe in a future where the privileged few can leave this planet, whether that’s through the Rapture, building bunkers and walled nations, or colonizing space and uploading brains into the cloud, Klein and Taylor detail the hard but satisfying work of those committed to staying on this planet and making a healthier and safer world for everyone who lives here.

While the book focuses primarily on global and national forces, Wilson’s participation in the conversation as the mayor of a large American city – which Klein said was a first such event for the writing duo – illustrated how the increasing national interest in the ideas of democratic socialism is playing out on the local stage.
The Urbanist's Fall Member Drive is in full swing! Support our work, read ad-free, and help us hit our goal for the member drive!

Americans have participated in widespread resistance to the tech elite through last year’s Tesla Takedown protests and this year’s pushback against the construction of data centers and the installation of Flock (and other) surveillance cameras , coupled with resistance to the ethno-nationalists with the rapid response and mutual aid networks deployed in defense of immigrants and the 2024 pushback in universities across the country to the religious extremists’ project of destruction and death in Gaza.
Americans have also shown their dissatisfaction with the status quo at the ballot box with the election of Zohran Mamdani in New York City and Katie Wilson in Seattle .
Klein spoke to Mamdani and Wilson’s shared love of their cities and cosmopolitan urbanism broadly as a strong message against the end times fascism described in the book.

“The very fact that cities are possible, and that diverse cities are possible, that people can live together, be curious about each other, be interested, realize that our lives are enriched precisely because of our differences, is the antithesis of fascism,” Klein said. “When people in cities say we love it here and run on these very positive visions, [...] where there's sort of love letters to the city and what makes them different and what makes them special, it reminds all of us that there's a reason why we live where we live.”
“I do believe cities are inherently anti-fascist,” Klein said.

After the introductory video, Wilson shared one line that particularly stuck out to her: “Fascism always emerges in moments of systemic crisis to protect elites from the threats of redistribution and accountability.”

Wilson provided a short summary of history from the post-Cold War 1990s during what she called “the peak of a certain version of neoliberal globalism,” a promise whose cracks began to show around the turn of the century with the rise of the anti-globalization movement.

“Fast forward to 2008, when I think the real systemic crisis began, and the Great Recession that followed that prompted Occupy here in the US, and that was really this recognition that that ‘rising tide lifts all boats’ was no longer believable here in the U.S.,” Wilson said. “There was now this whole generation of young people who realized that they were having less economic security than their parents did, and that kind of loss of legitimacy of the status quo really opened up space for the growth of new left movements, including that mainstreaming of democratic socialism that we're seeing today.”
Wilson observed that the crisis of legitimacy that began in 2008 has only deepened and contributed to the worldwide political polarization we’re currently living through.
Seattle has a bit of an uneasy relationship with big tech and the tech oligarchs that Klein and Taylor call out as a current fascist force.

In 2024, Seattle ranked second among the 50 largest U.S. cities for its share of tech workers, with 13.3% of its employed workers being in tech. As of the end of 2024, 23% of the country’s AI engineers lived in Seattle , a number only topped in the San Francisco Bay Area. And Anthropic , one of the country’s leading AI firms, signed a lease this summer for a 113,000-square-foot space in Seattle.

Meanwhile, about 70% of JumpStart payroll expense tax payments come from just 10 companies, most of them in the technology sector, including Amazon, Mega, Google, and Expedia. As of 2026, the first tier of the Jumpstart tax kicked in at $194,452 in individual annual compensation, with the tax paid only on the portion in excess. The City of Seattle has depended on the JumpStart tax to balance its budget since it began being collected in 2021.

At the same time, Seattle’s City Council passed a one-year moratorium on constructing new data centers within the city limits earlier this year. And while the council as a whole has supported increasing police surveillance in the city, that effort has met with local resistance . The mood around the rise of AI as touted by the tech oligarchs, similar to around the country, has been mixed even as Klein and Taylor’s book names and shames these oligarchs as playing a major role in the current fascist push.
Wilson acknowledged this tension on stage at the book talk.

“I feel like there's a lot of complexity here for all of us living in one of the big tech capitals of the world, and I have a lot of chance to reflect on this as the mayor, thinking about how AI and other technologies that are being developed really do have the potential to improve human life, but they also come with huge risks, and there are real questions about responsible use, especially in a profit-driven economy,” Wilson said. “And all of us in Seattle, and especially maybe me as mayor, are in this complicated position because also our workforce, our residents, and our city budget depend on high-wage tech jobs, and so I've done a lot thinking about what is my role as mayor and all of our roles in growing an economy that's as life affirming as possible, and it's a challenge.”

Wilson recently released an executive order with plans to convene a "Resilient Seattle Economy Task Force,” make regulatory and permitting changes to to make it easier to start and grow businesses, and direct the Seattle Strategic Initiatives Fund to develop a proposal to “explore tools” to help diversify the City’s economy.

“We need to get to the political economy,” Taylor responded to Wilson’s assertion of complexity. “Who owns it? Are we making investments in the things humans need so that the tech, if we use it, serves us?”
When considering the ethno-nationalist prong of the fascist alliance posited in the book, Wilson brought up Trump’s immigration policies.

“Here in King County, our population growth, our economic growth is really driven by international immigration,” Wilson said. “If you look at the numbers, it is astounding. I think in the last five years, we would have a net outflow of population if you didn't count really significant international immigration, and so then when the Trump administration starts aggressively restricting H-1B visas, then that threatens that kind of pipeline, and so it's this very self-defeating kind of posture.”
Wilson was clear about the antidote against the political movement pushing for different versions of the end times.

“What we need to do is we need to have that credible, hopeful, inclusive vision for what the future can be, and we have to trust that people will go for that, and then we have to actually deliver it,” Wilson said.

This remark echoed both what Wilson said on the campaign trail and what she said about her recent executive order designed to promote government efficiency and budget sustainability: that her mission is to show that local government can deliver. Wilson also discussed an opportunity she sees on the left to take over the “adult in the room” persona that has long been the province of the rightwing in the US.

“With Trump, that's just totally fallen apart,” Wilson said. “You have this extreme fiscal irresponsibility that is paired with wholesale destruction of core government functions, and I think that really opens up the space for the left to be the adult in the room and recapture some of that language and maturity in a way that can allow us to put together governing coalitions that can really be effective.”

Klein and Taylor discussed Wilson’s mayoral win last fall in the book, using it as an example that Mamdani’s victory in New York City was neither singular nor too liberal to succeed elsewhere and quoting from Wilson’s inaugural speech .

“Wilson was a very different kind of politician: a long-time transit activist, she's a little geeky and not a natural performer," the authors wrote. “But like Mamdani, her platform emphasized affordability, including quality social housing and accessible childcare, and it challenged local billionaires’ agenda for the city. Seattle is a tech stronghold, and Wilson questioned the wisdom of keeping the city dependent on a sector racing toward world-burning AI and banking on a post-human future. She put economic diversification and sustainability on the ballot.”

While Wilson is taking a small step forward toward economic diversification with the recent executive order outlined above, it is hard to say how much she will ultimately challenge the city’s billionaires. For example, Amazon gave a statement to KIRO Newsradio last week supporting her recent budget proposal .

What remains clear is Wilson’s commitment to cities in general, and to the City of Seattle in particular, as she gushed about how cities are humanity’s greatest invention. She explained that her “this is your city” tagline expresses a message of belonging, participation, and collective responsibility to one another.

“We have a shared responsibility to each other and to the city that we share, and so, to me, that really is the antithesis of end times,” Wilson said. “It's about what we can create together in a way that is inclusive and that's life affirming. And I feel like cities are a place where we can really do that.”

articles.title: Group Dynamics
articles.author: Dan Savage
paras: I’m a 37-year-old (mostly) straight man who has been in and out of a series of committed, monogamous relationships for most of my adult life. I’m now at a point where I am feeling torn in two, and it doesn’t seem like there’s anyone in my life who I can ask for help who won’t judge me. I am getting old, and I want to have kids. I have always known I wanted to have kids, but it just hasn’t happened yet, mostly because I keep moving for my career and I stayed in some long-distance relationships longer than I should have.

I’m also more and more possessed by a desire to have group sex. This has always been a small idea in the back of my head. But as I’ve grown older, the more obsessed I am with the idea. I dream about FFM threesomes, as so many men do, but lately I’m also into the idea of MMF threesomes as well as having sex in a large, mixed-gender group.

I’ve started seeing a sweet and wonderful woman fresh out of a divorce who has one kid and wants more. But I recently learned that one of the main reasons her marriage broke up is that her ex was into group sex. There was more to their divorce than just that, of course, but her ex’s desire for group sex played a big role. This is a relationship I could really see working in the long run, and it would give me the chance to finally have the family I’ve always dreamed of. But I worry that even bringing up my interest in group sex would make her run for the hills. I’m terrified that I’ve already betrayed her just by continuing to see her — I have not cheated — and conversely, I’m afraid that I’m setting myself up for a life without this thing that has totally consumed my erotic imagination. But if we break up, I’m terrified I’ll miss my chance to have a family, and that seems so much more important than what I find myself thinking of as “just a silly sex thing.”

I’m terrified to even tell my close friends about this because I’m sure they’ll think I’m either a pervert or completely insane for hesitating to marry this woman for this reason. But then I don’t have anybody to talk to. I’m even afraid to broach the subject with a therapist.
We all face, as grown-ass adults, hard choices between competing wannas.

If you wanna be with this woman and start a family, you may not be able to realize your fantasies about group sex. If you wanna act on those fantasies — if you don’t wanna go to your grave without ever having had group sex — you probably won’t be able to start a family with this woman.
That doesn’t mean you can’t date her, COWARD, but you do need to level with her, and soon.

Zooming out for a second: You shouldn’t feel like a freak for having fantasies about group sex, COWARD, and this woman shouldn’t feel like the universe is picking on her by putting another man in her life who fantasizes about group sex. Group sex is an extremely common fantasy! Dr. Justin Lehmiller’s extensive research on people’s sexual interests found that fantasies about threesomes — FFM, MMF, MMM, FFF — are widespread, COWARD, as are fantasies about sex in groups of four or more. We’re talking landslide numbers: 95% of men and 87% of women have fantasized about threesomes, according to Dr. Lehmiller’s research, and upwards of 75% of everybody has fantasized about sex in even larger groups. Which means that anyone this woman dates — statistically speaking — is highly likely to have fantasies about group sex. So, if being with someone who even fantasizes about group sex would send this woman running to the hills, COWARD, she should consider relocating to hill country permanently.

Zooming out a little further: People like to pretend that a sexual fantasy — common or niche — is “just a silly sex thing,” COWARD, especially people who can easily find sexual fulfillment in conventional monogamous relationships, e.g. straight vanilla people. But many kinky people feel self-conscious about their “silly sex things” and don’t feel entitled to prioritize their own sexual fulfillment. No one vanilla or kinky gets everything they want, of course, and everyone has to balance sexual fulfillment and compatibility against other competing priorities, like emotional compatibility, marriage, children, etc., but you have as much right to ask the universe (and your girlfriend) for what you want as any vanilla person does.

We are all entitled to a zone of erotic autonomy — yadda yadda yadda — and no one is obligated to share every desire with a potential partner. We aren’t obligated to disclose every sexual interest and/or obsession to a potential partner. But I would strongly encourage you to disclose your group sex fantasies to this woman, COWARD, if for no other reason than to avoid her finding out on her own. If you tell her now and she runs for the hills, she’ll be upset but she’ll get over it (and over you) while she’s up there. But if she finds out on her own after you’ve had a couple kids — because you forgot to clear your browser history or you blurted it out after your first colonoscopy (coming out from under the anesthesia is a trip ) — she’s likely to feel a betrayal so profound that it could tear the family you created with her apart. Knowing you have these fantasies doesn’t mean she has to help you realize them, COWARD, but you shouldn’t be ashamed of them and you don’t want to live with the stress of wondering how she’ll feel when (not if) she finds out.

You say you found out the role group sex played in her divorce recently, COWARD, and it’s understandable that you needed some time to think about how to share this with her. But the longer you wait to tell her, the more emotionally manipulative you’re going to appear when you finally do tell her and/or she finds out on her own. You want to get out in front of this.

P.S. You are not insane and you’re not a pervert — or if you are, COWARD, you have lots of company. If this relationship ends, finding another woman who 1. wants a family and 2. is open to group sex isn’t the terrifyingly impossible task you imagine it to be.

P.P.S. I don’t want to give you false hopes, but there’s a chance that it wasn’t the group sex itself — or the group sex by itself — that she hated about her ex. Did he pressure her to engage in group sex in situations that made her uncomfortable or with people that gave her the ick?
P.P.P.S. Please get a therapist — start your search at AASECT — and broach this subject ASAP.

I’m a gay man pushing forty, and I’ve been with my partner for nearly twenty wonderful, open years. We have a deep, loving foundation, but a recent dry spell coupled with a new face has me spiraling. Lately, my boyfriend has been seeing a 20-year-old boy. Unlike our usual one-offs, this thing has lasted for more than six months and it involves a lot of regular chatting and it looks a lot like they’re dating to me. To make it worse, my partner initially lied about it. Around the same time, he’s had trouble staying hard with me. While we shrugged it off and cuddled in the moment, but I’m being eaten alive by the fear that he’s comparing me to the “younger model” and preparing to replace me with him. I know pressuring him about his performance will only backfire so I have kept my feelings to myself and when it’s just the two of us, we are still as loving and affectionate as ever. Am I overthinking a standard dry spell or is this “hookup” turning into something that genuinely threatens our future?
First: I’m going to refer to your partner’s 20-year-old sidepiece as a “boy.” But he is, in a point of fact, a man. A young man, and a much younger man, but a man.

Moving on: However enamored your partner might be of this boy, TOM, here’s hoping your partner isn’t foolish enough to blow up his life (and yours) for a boy who can’t legally buy a beer. At best, TOM, your partner will be an early, brief, and hopefully positive chapter in this boy’s life — and if your partner isn’t a fool, TOM, he not only knows that himself, he’s communicated that to this boy. (If your partner is making promises he can’t keep and/or filling this boy with false hopes about a future together, he’s violating the Campsite Rule .)

While people in long-ass-term relationships sometimes fantasize about different timelines and/or different partners (see my response to PAIN in last week’s column ), TOM, those fantasies are usually idle and fleeting. So, while your partner is obviously into this boy, TOM, and while your partner may have fantasized about an alternative, it doesn’t follow that your partner is preparing to replace you with him.

I’m not gonna sugarcoat this next part: your partner is probably more excited about fucking this boy than he is about fucking you, TOM, but that doesn’t mean your partner loves you any less . It only means that this boy is shiny and new. And while sex with a long-term partner is rewarding in ways that sex with someone you’ve just met can never be, sex with someone new is exciting in ways that sex with someone you’ve been fucking for twenty years can never be. But that’s not something I need to tell you, is it? At some point over the twenty years you’ve been in this open relationship, TOM, you must have experienced the same kind of new relationship energy with someone else — even if that new relationship only lasted a few hours.

Nothing I’ve said excuses your partner lying to you, TOM, and people in open relationships should go out of their way — they should lean into — offering reassurances to their long-term partners. But your partner’s biggest failing, I think, is the way he seems to have taken advantage of some ambiguity in your open relationship. While sex outside your relationship always consisted of one-offs before this boy came along — no repeats — it doesn’t sound like that was ever a formal rule. So, while you’ve been operating under the assumption that repeats weren’t allowed because repeats never happened, your partner is operating under the assumption that repeats were allowed — or conveniently began operating under that assumption about sex months ago — because repeats weren’t specifically disallowed.

That’s not an assumption he should’ve made. Even if the two of you never articulated a rule against repeats and/or the kind of connection he has with this boy, TOM, your partner should’ve checked in with you — and gotten your permission — before this boy became a fixture in your lives. Instead, he lied and/or minimized and/or rationalized his actions and damaged your sense of security (in this relationship) and trust (in him).

So, you need to get on the same page about the rules going forward. You’ll either need to agree on rules that allow for other boyfriends — and what your partner is doing with this boy sounds very boyfriendy — or you’ll need to agree on rules that disallow for other boyfriends. If your partner agrees to a “no repeats, no dating, no other boyfriends” rule going forward, he’ll need to end things with this boy. If he can’t do that, TOM, or you don’t wanna make him do that, he’ll have to promise you that once this boy moves on from him, which he inevitably will, there will never be another boy like him.

P.S. It sounds like you’re reading way too much into one lost erection. Your partner not being able to get it up with you one night isn’t proof your partner isn’t into you — and for all you know, TOM, your partner has had the same problem with this boy. He is getting older, right?

Single female here . I was on my own for six months before I made a “friend with benefits.” We’d meet up two or three times a week. We’d talk, have a gummy, drink, and spend the night together — nothing more. We had been doing this for nearly two years when I met a guy and started seeing him seriously. We get along great, we play sports together, we go away for long weekends, etc. I had been wanting a partner like this and he was a perfect fit. Here is the problem: sex with my partner is almost non-existent. He has ED and does not like taking Viagra or its alternatives. So, we sometimes we go two or three weeks without doing anything sexual. I have resorted to seeing my FWB at least once a week. My actual partner can never find out about this, as he would be devastated. He’s not open to any alternatives to monogamy. I know cheating on him is wrong and that this could blow up in my face. But we are so happy together that I don’t know what to do. Should I walk away before he finds out? It would crush my partner if he knew. I would rather leave him than tell him. Advice for me?
P.S. He did ask me once if I was sleeping with anyone else, and I lied and said no, as I knew his expectation for me is to be just with him.

articles.title: Why Can’t Seattle Fund the Arts Like It’s FIFA Every Year?
articles.author: Amanda Manitach
paras: There’s a draft of an open letter to Mayor Katie Wilson and the Seattle City Council that’s been making the rounds on social media and racking up signatures over the past few days. The request: divert $8 million from SPD’s $68 million proposed budget increase and give that money to the arts. The reasoning? Art activations and cultural programming placed throughout the city should be considered a form of public-safety infrastructure.

It’s a compelling argument, particularly in light of Wilson’s newly released 2027–28 proposed budget , which purports to prioritize “stability, safety, and affordability,” with more than half of its total $9.1 billion in proposed spending allocated to public safety.

The letter, drafted by a group of Seattle artists, cultural workers, and community stakeholders and spearheaded by artist and community organizer Julie Chang Schulman, was published as a Google document last Tuesday. It points to Seattle’s 2026 World Cup-related arts events as evidence of what that scale of art funding can accomplish. According to the city , $3.6 million was distributed through 120 grants that supported 80 public art projects and cultural activations. Of that amount, $2.3 million was earmarked by the Office of Arts & Culture (OAC) for specifically FIFA-related summer events . Those investments paid off over the summer, the letter argues, with community-led public activations contributing to Seattle’s first zero-homicide June since 1970 .

“This summer proved a critical reality: art and cultural placemaking is public safety infrastructure,” the letter states. “Such a massive expansion of the SPD budget is the wrong approach, particularly when the department is not suffering from a lack of resources, but rather from a bottleneck created by its own union’s policies.”

The letter specifically points to the ongoing efforts of the Seattle Police Officers Guild (SPOG) to hinder the efficacy of the Community Assisted Response and Engagement (CARE) Department, an unarmed police alternative that responds to non-violent 911 calls. Despite Wilson’s support of CARE—under her administration, the number of CARE responders has jumped from 24 to 40— SPOG continues to weaponize its contract to limit the types of calls CARE can respond to, claiming that it takes away from police jobs. The letter argues that community-based safety measures—including art programs and activations—conducted by trusted community members don’t merely put a Band-Aid on the problem; they work to intervene at the root, breaking cycles of violence.

The letter does not mince words: “We have a better model right in front of us. If we can fund community activation for FIFA and our summer tourists, we can—and must—do it for the people who call Seattle home year-round.”

Schulman, who has been sharing the document on Instagram, is active in the local arts and civic community. She is co-executive steward at Forever Safe Spaces / On The Block Seattle , founder of Seattle Artist Coalition for Equitable Development , and co-chair of the Capitol Hill Arts District steering committee.

The letter has drawn nearly 400 individual signers at the time of publication, spanning Seattle’s arts and cultural community as well as organizers, small-business owners, educators, and community advocates.

For Schulman, the argument is grounded in first-hand experience. Organizations she works with, including On the Block, received increased support through the city’s 2026 arts funding, distributed via the Capitol Hill Arts District.

“But this convo isn’t about one org,” Schulman told me over Instagram. “The impact in our direct community was transformative, [but most] activations were limited to Pioneer Square. Imagine if they were not limited to [the] World Cup [and] downtown, and artists and orgs could activate in place?” Schulman imagines what an art activation proposal could do in Little Saigon, a neighborhood where violent crime has increased in the last few years. She’s confident the neighborhood has “community members with creative solutions” who lack resources to implement them.
What could $8 million actually buy the community?

The amount would be more than double OAC’s 2025–26 funding for these type of placemaking projects—things like farmers-market-style events, Pride festivals and watch parties, community cycling activations, and guided walking tours by Vanishing Seattle / Street Trees of Seattle—extending the reach of such an investment well beyond downtown. The letter doesn’t specify exactly how the $8 million might be distributed, but we can surmise. For context, the current Arts in Parks program offers individual awards ranging from $2,000 to $8,000. At $8,000 per grant, $8 million could theoretically fund 1,000 grants. At $2,000 per grant, it could fund 4,000. (For reference, in 2026, Arts in Parks funded 33 grants , with a total budget of $216,000.)
That’s a lot of artists. But is redirecting $8 million from SPD’s budget actually feasible?

Eight million dollars represents around a measly 1.4 percent of SPD’s proposed annual $556 million budget—an increase of 14 percent compared to 2025. However, most of that budget increase is already spoken for. Approximately $53.8 million would go toward the costs associated with the recently negotiated SPOG contract , including wage increases. A large chunk of the rest—approximately $12.6 million—would go toward fully funding 66 officers hired in 2026, whose salaries were not accounted for in this year’s budget.

The desired $8 million would likely need to be absorbed through cuts made elsewhere throughout the SPD. Budget cuts made in the summer of 2020 —including reductions in sworn patrol officers and recruitment spending—demonstrated it’s more than possible to trim the fat when there’s a will.

The overarching question is straightforward: If the city is willing to spend millions on public safety, what counts as public-safety spending? And what if some of that money went toward creating the conditions that make people want to be in public spaces in the first place?

Even without the hypothetical $8 million in redirected funds, there’s some good news for the arts in Wilson’s budget. She protected existing arts funding from being cut to help address the $175 million general fund budget deficit. Instead, the proposal includes additional funding for the OAC over the biennium, including an increase in grant awards to account for the rising cost of living for artists (cheers, all around), expanded funding for Creative Advantage (arts education in Seattle Public Schools), additional money to maintain the Civic Art Collection, and one-time funding to continue the arts programing at King Street Station.

That’s great. (I can hear audible sighs of relief wafting from King Street.) But the letter makes an argument that seems pretty damn reasonable: If the mayor’s budget recognizes that arts programming is worth protecting—and even expanding—why can’t Seattle make a World Cup-scale investment in local arts an ongoing strategy, rather than a one-off game plan designed around sports tourism?

Back in March, I wrote about Mayor Katie Wilson’s Arts, Culture, and Creative Economy Transition Team and their ambitious but not-at-all-crazy ideas for generating increased funding for the arts. Among the team’s goals (and a constant quest for policymakers and artists alike) was finding ways to cement Seattle’s civic identity as an arts city.

Putting money where your mouth is—by putting money directly into artists’ hands—is the most effective way to do that. Artists don’t have a guild like SPOG to advocate for hundreds of millions of dollars on their behalf. If Seattle is serious about thinking of public safety as more than police response, then the letter’s authors are posing a serious question that deserves a real conversation. Is Seattle going to treat the $3.6 million it spent on World Cup-related creative placemaking as an exceptional expense, or is it a preview of what a city that actually wants to be an arts city might look like year-round?

articles.title: Slog AM: If You Love Trains and Hate the Mariners Coaching Staff, Boy, Have I got Good News for You
articles.author: Hunter Pauli
paras: Suspect in Juniper Blessing killing still not competent to stand trial: He’ll remain in treatment for now, a judge ruled Monday. KUOW has details on his specific issues.

Governor Bob Ferguson hasn’t commuted the prison sentence of a single person: According to Investigate West , a board appointed by Ferguson has recommended early release for 15 people, none of which Ferguson has followed through on. Washington legislators abolished parole for most inmates in 1984, leaving few avenues for early release other than the governor’s mercy. So far, Ferguson has shown none.

Amtrak’s Seattle-Portland route finally gets trains built this century: It feels like the Carter administration in a lot of ways right now—skyrocketing oil prices, plummeting popularity for the president over a botched invasion of Iran—but for Amtrak Cascades riders, the future is finally here. No, not high speed rail, but passenger train cars so new they don’t even have ashtrays in the arm rests. They leave the station for the first time tomorrow .

Seattle got a new light rail station, too and the Seattle Times absolutely hates it, judging by their recent reporting . The city failed to build up a dense new community around the Pinehurst station during planning and construction, so it may be underutilized until developers realize this (there is a tempting looking golf course to bulldoze right next door). This has of course infuriated Ballard residents who think they deserve light rail more than Pinehurst residents, but there’s no word yet from Sound Transit on my modest proposal to build the new line to Magnolia Village instead and ignore Ballard voices.

Mariners purge coaching staff: It probably has something to do with them leading the team to a terrible fucking season a year after they won the AL West Championship for the first time in a generation and got everyone’s hopes up. As a lifelong local Mariners fan I recognized this ruse for what it was a mile away and knew not to look on the bright side, but a lot of people fell for the trick and now the team is out its manager, hitting coach, infield coach, bench coach, and more.
COVID and flu cases are rising in Seattle, KUOW reports , but there’s simply no way of knowing why. Unrelated video below.

Several Washington races set to shape collaboration between ICE and local law enforcement: A recent nationwide roundup of elections that will change how effectively ICE can deport people in local communities published by Bolts highlights Pierce County in particular, where the far-right “constitutional sheriff” Keith Swank has made few friends by actively cooperating with ICE contrary to state law and threatening the legislature. Pierce County voters will decide this November whether to amend the county charter to make the sheriff an appointed position rather than elected, allowing commissioners to replace Swank.

Microsoft shutters the team that botched Halo for years: 343 Studios, later renamed Halo Studios, never quite had the magic touch that original developers Bungie did. After 15 years of rough launches, bad art design, and a falling consumer base, Microsoft has pulled the plug and is handing the franchise over to Activision, which will put together a development team. Like Bungie, Halo Studios is a local company, which means hundreds more Washington tech sector layoffs for Microsoft.

Minimum wage is going up, kinda: It’ll be $22.14 in Seattle starting next year, which looks to be a bit under inflation according to the Seattle Times , meaning effectively a small pay cut if costs stay high.

Further proof Netanyahu was warned of October 7 attacks and did nothing: Egypt’s intelligence chief personally chartered a Cessna jet to Tel Aviv to warn the Israelis of Hamas’ plans, The Atlantic reports .

Everyone’s favorite Weimar Republic detective show’s new season is premiering now: Babylon Berlin season 5 starts with the Nazis taking power so the showrunners are running out of time to wrap things up for our characters before everybody presumably dies. That’s not a spoiler by the way, you can’t spoil WWII. We probably won’t get the new season streaming on our shores next year, which makes me confused as to what our continued occupation of Germany is even getting us.

articles.title: Everett Link Draft EIS Review
articles.author: Wesley Lin
paras: On September 18, Sound Transit released the Environmental impact Statement for the Everett Link extension . This light rail extension will extend the Link light rail system north towards Everett from Lynnwood. The first phase plans to build the West Alderwood , Ash Way , Mariner , and finally the SW Everett Industrial Center by 2037. The second phase would extend it north to Everett with SR 526/Evergreen and Everett Station by 2041. There is also one unfunded provisional station at SR 99/Airport Road .
The draft EIS comment period is open until November 2nd.

This article will mostly focus on the first phase up to SW Everett Industrial Center. Most of the station alignments were previously discussed in The Urbanist as well. This discussion will focus on the details of the preferred options. Unless otherwise cited, all images are from the Sound Transit online open house .
From Lynnwood station, the line would continue north along the west side of I-5 then turn east near 33rd Ave W.

Among the alternatives considered, the preferred alternative is ALD-2D (Northern Mall Alignment with 33rd Avenue Station) shown in green. The first stop is West Alderwood next to Alderwood Mall. High retail activity and surrounding apartments should drive strong ridership.
The ALD-2D option will place the elevated station to the west of Alderwood Mall next to the JC Penney.
For the preferred alternative of ALD-D the three bus routes of 121, 122, and Swift orange would stop there. For the other alternatives of ALD-B and ALD-F the Swift Orange bus might skip the station.

There are some alternative options moving the station to the north or south of Alderwood Mall instead. Most of them have moderate tradeoffs with which properties would need to displaced. All of them would cost approximately the same at $1 billion.

From Alderwood Mall, the line would the continue north along I-5. There is no preferred alternative for this segment. The Ash Way station would be near the 164th St SW and I-5 intersection. The Swift Orange BRT would help connect residents along 164th St SW to the station. The line would reuse the existing Ash Way Park-and-Ride for parking.
ASH-1A (West of I-5 Alignment with Ash Way Park-and-Ride Station) has the line staying west of I-5. This would build the elevated Ash Way station next to the Ash Way Park-and-Ride.

The other option ASH-2D (East of I-5 Alignment with 164th Street Station) would build it on the east of I-5. One complication is that this would be complicated for the station to connect to the existing west transit facilities.
Snohomish County explored fixing the east station issues with the I-5/164th St SW Direct Access Improvements project to build an HOV/pedestrian bridge just north of 164th Street.
Assuming the I-5 overpass is built, the routes 112, 121, m103, 117, n14 and m2 will terminate at Ash Way. Swift Orange line will also using the crossing and continue along it.

The option ASH-1A staying on the west of I-5 supposedly costs more than ASH-2D. However, I’m somewhat skeptical of the numbers considering ASH-2D requires an expensive bridge across I-5 while ASH-1A stays on the same side.
After Ash Way, the line will continue north along I-5 to the Mariner Station. Clusters of garden-style apartments along 128th St SW will generate strong residential ridership.
The MAR-1B (South of 128th Street Alignment with 8th Avenue Station) alternative will build the elevated Mariner station just south of 128th St SW.
The Mariner station would serve as the transfer point for many bus routes around South Everett.
The Swift Orange will likely be extended one mile and terminate at Mariner Station instead of its current terminus at McCollum P&R.

Once the line reaches Mariner, the train will then head west along Airport Road. There is the provisional unfunded SR 99 / Airport Road station at the intersection. This SR 99 / Airport Road is surrounded by mostly light industrial and commercial properties however it would also be a pretty vital half-way point transfer point for the Swift Blue BRT line.

The SW Everett Industrial Center station (a somewhat laborious way to say Boeing) will be built near Paine Field and the Everett Boeing factory. There has been some competing priorities of whether to build this station on the north nearby Boeing for the workers or whether to build it to the west near Paine Field for passengers.
The SWI-1A (Airport Road/SR 526 Alignment with SR 526 Station) is the preferred Alternative. This would place it closest to the Seaway Transit center that Boeing workers currently use.
One complication is that most of the buses would have to take a circuitous route to reach the Seaway Transit Center. A pedestrian bridge might be built to connect the station to Boeing across SR 526.

The SWI-1B alternative places it in the mid point between the airport and Boeing. While the SWI-1C alternative places the station closest to the airport. Also interestingly, there would be an airport shuttle bus with all three station sites from the station to Paine Field airport.
These next two stations will be built in a later phase by 2041.
After SW Everett Industrial Center, the line will continue east along SR 526 to SR 526/Evergreen station. There are five alternatives here with much community pushback. We’ll go over EGN-A and EGN-E.

The EGN-A alternative will place it just north of the SR 526 freeway with the least property impacts. This places it closer to apartments such as the Four Corners and the Cascade High School. A pedestrian bridge will be built to make it easier to cross south of the freeway. However, it is also tricky to transfer to some buses.
The EGN-E places it just south of W Casino Road.
Both alternatives would connect to the Swift Blue and the future Swift Silver Line (labeled as a rerouted Green Line above).
One advantage of the EGN-E station closer to Casino Ave, is that it is easier for a bus to reach Everett Mall.
The main preferred alternative is EVT-1A (Smith Avenue Alignment) which places the Everett light rail station closest to the existing Sounder Everett station.
EVT-A would be an elevated station at the corner of Smith Ave and 32nd St.

Sound Transit has not yet decided where to place the new Operations and Maintenance Facility (OMF). One of the above three spots will be picked. The OMF is used for train maintenance, cleaning, and storage.

The projected ridership with the initial phase (in green) and second phase (in pink) is shown above. The highest daily ridership is projected at Everett Station with 10,700 riders. The next two highest are Ash Way and Mariner with approximately 4,600 riders. Mariner would have an estimated 7,000 riders (2,400 more) with the initial phase due to I-5 freeway buses from Everett truncating there.

The Everett Link extension will mostly benefit trips within the Everett and North Lynnwood area and not improve the freeway trips between Everett and destinations south of Lynnwood. Sound Transit estimates 29 minutes from Lynnwood station to Everett station which is on par with the current freeway bus times.

The original operating plan for the ST3 calls for the 3 Line to serve all stations between Lynnwood and Everett. In addition, the 2 Line will be extended to Mariner station. During peak hours, Sound Transit plans to provide 3 minute frequency for the West Alderwood, Ash Way, and Mariner stations. North of Mariner, frequency will drop to 6 minutes.

With the phased implementation plan, the exact operation plan is not clear. In addition, the exact lines that serve the new stations will also depend on the opening timelines for other ST3 extensions to West Seattle and Ballard.

articles.title: Clyde Hill Brokers Deal to Settle Growth Plan Complaint
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: The tucked-away enclave of Clyde Hill is poised to create a new affordable housing incentive program, prompted by a legal challenge that city leaders have been attempting to settle for over a year. The modest tweak to its land use code, considered at a public hearing last week at the Clyde Hill planning commission, would grant property owners slightly more building rights in exchange for furthering the city's state-mandated affordable housing requirements.

Clyde Hill officials are set to sign onto this idea, slightly chipping away at the stringent zoning requirements that the city has touted for decades, in order to avoid a state growth board ruling that could potentially tear apart that armor even further. The adjustment illustrates the ways that relatively recent changes in state law continue to prompt even Washington's most exclusive jurisdictions to make moves to respond to a statewide housing shortage and affordability crisis.
The Urbanist's Fall Member Drive is in full swing! Support our work, read ad-free, and help us hit our goal for the member drive!

Last April, the land use advocacy nonprofit Futurewise filed an appeal against Clyde Hill's newly adopted Comprehensive Plan, targeting shortcomings that mirrored those alleged in the group's appeal of the growth plan in nearby Mercer Island . The appeal asserted that Clyde Hill had failed "to document programs and actions needed to achieve housing availability including gaps in local funding," responding to a 2021 law that requires cities to plan for future residents across all income bands, among other requirements.
If Clyde Hill is able to reach a settlement, it will avoid having to defend its entire growth framework at a hearing at the state's Growth Management Hearings Board.

"We haven't had that hearing yet because shortly after the growth board challenge was brought by Futurewise, we entered into settlement discussions with them, and have been trying to create a compromise where maybe they don't get everything they're asking for in their petition," Clyde Hill City Attorney Jeff Taraday said Thursday. "But we change at least some of what they want us to change, and then as a result of that, we avoid having to actually have that hearing before the board, which is costly and, as with any litigation, fraught with some amount of uncertainty."

For a small city like Clyde Hill, with a median income of around $483,000 and virtually no land zoned for multifamily housing, the idea of "making adequate provisions" for households making a fraction of that amount has been a confounding one. Through 2044, the city has been required to plan for 10 new units of housing, a modest target in scale, but all of those units are aimed at households making less than 100% of broader King County's area median income (AMI), with three of those units targeted at households making less than 30% of AMI – approximately $40,000 for a family of two. Those type of units only get built with significant public subsidy.

Under the plan that was forwarded to the Clyde Hill Council by its Planning Commission Thursday, property owners who agree to build an accessory dwelling unit (ADU) on their property that is rented to a household earning at or below 50% of King County's area median income for a period of 20 years would be able to increase structural lot coverage – the amount of space on a lot taken up by buildings – from the 30% cap currently in the code to 40%.

Alternatively, that 40% structural lot coverage could be achieved by paying a fee "in lieu" of building the unit, of a flat $400,000. Those funds would then be collected by the city and used to subsidize affordable units elsewhere, likely outside the city via A Regional Coalition for Housing (ARCH) .

The initial proposal, presented to the planning commission in August, also had additional building rights in the package, including a decreased rear-yard setback (from 35 feet to 20) and a decreased side-yard setback (from 15 feet to 10) on lots larger than 1,500 square feet. In addition, detached ADUs would have been allowed to rise to 25 feet tall compared to the current 12 feet. But those provisions ended up on the cutting room floor, in large part due to concerns over potential impacts on neighboring properties.

"I would rather live next door to a house that is a little bigger than I thought it was going to be than I would live next door to a house that is now five feet closer to me," commission chair Jared Wheeler said last month.
After scaling back the program to only include lot coverage, the proposal now appears to be viewed as the type of pill that Clyde Hill can swallow to get into compliance with state law.

"I sympathize with the concern about people's views being affected, but the state has mandated that we do more for affordable housing, this isn't our choice, and it appears that the majority of the burden is going to fall on the people who choose to either move here and build or build new houses," commissioner Spencer Hamlin said during Thursday's hearing.
Clyde Hill policymakers admitted they would like to mandate protection of views for homeowners, but that they realize state law likely precludes that approach.

"I think that the view encroachment is not good, but it's something that the people with existing houses are going to have to shoulder and bear, essentially, as part of them also accepting that this is the consequence of the state law," Hamlin said. "How do we spread out, fairly, all of the costs of this? I don't want my view encroached on either. Nobody does, but I don't see a reasonable scenario where you could do this and mandate protection of views. You'd have to blow up our building code."

So where did the $400,000 number, which one planning commissioner referred to a a developer's "golden ticket" to build a larger house on a lot in Clyde Hill, come from? Clyde Hill City Administrator Heather Thomas-Murphy said that it was developed in conjunction with ARCH, and is roughly tied to the cost to build one unit of affordable housing in the region.

"There's a lot of variables around the dollar amounts, but in general, they said $400,000 would be a justifiable number," Thomas-Murphy said. "The question is, what type of unit are we building, and where are we building it? It's more expensive to build in Clyde Hill than it is in some of our neighboring properties, but they said $400,000 was a good start."
A motion to lower the fee to $200,000 died at last week's meeting for lack of a second.
Thomas-Murphy told commissioners that Futurewise had indicated "conceptual support" for the proposal.

"With settlement discussions ongoing, we're limited in what we can say about the City's draft," Futurewise spokesperson Cat Huber told The Urbanist, instead pointing to the public ruling against Mercer Island from last summer. "Since HB 1220 , a city must identify land capacity for housing at each income level rather than in aggregate. Wherever a city counts on incentives or voluntary programs to produce that housing, the record must show how many units, at what income levels, or how much revenue those incentives can be expected to generate."

Futurewise sees its role as a "leading statewide public interest watchdog and legal steward of Washington's Growth Management Act" or GMA, which state lawmakers passed in 1990 to rein in suburban sprawl.

"Mercer Island's compliance filing, which is public, shows the kind of analysis that was put in that record," Huber continued. "That is the framework that applies to any jurisdiction's program, whatever form it takes. Futurewise continues to work collaboratively with Clyde Hill on solutions that meet GMA housing requirements and contribute to long-term community wellbeing."

Over its three plus decades of existence, the GMA has been relatively effective at limiting sprawl , but it's taken recent reforms to boost effectiveness at encouraging dense housing development within the urban growth boundary the law generated.

Clyde Hill is far from the only city getting nudged in this way. Futurewise is also negotiating a potential settlement with nearby Hunts Point, while the state's Department of Commerce remains in negotiations with Duvall after that city's Comprehensive Plan tried to sidestep many of these new requirements entirely. Meanwhile, the 2025 Housing Accountability Act created a new avenue of direct state review of housing growth plans, entirely outside of the Growth Management Hearings Board process.
The Clyde Hill City Council is expected to formally take up the affordable housing incentive program in November.

articles.title: What Will Become of the Empress Tree?
articles.author: Meg van Huygen
paras: Taha Ebrahimi, professional tree nerd and author of Trees of Seattle: An Illustrated Walking Guide , sent a DM to our friend group chat on Wednesday morning.

“You guys!!! Vacilando is closing this Saturday!!!!! 😭😭😭😢” Ebrahimi included a link to Capitol Hill Blog’s story from the night before, which reported that the crumbling century-old building, which houses Bar Vacilando, Rione XIII, and Rubenstein Bagels, has been forced into vacancy due to ongoing structural and financial issues. The other shops closed immediately; Vacilando shuttered on Saturday, September 26.
My response, after “God fucking damn it,” was:

Bar Vacilando was lovely for many reasons, including its high ceilings, clean lines, herb-dusted fries with dippy garlic-curry aioli, and lightweight cherry tomato-infused martinis. But the jewel in its crown is doubtlessly the tiny patio’s 20-foot Paulownia tomentosa, aka the empress tree. The patio is conceptually inseparable from this sprawling and flamboyant tree, which grows from the brick foundation of the building next door, forming a leafy umbrella over the tables and blooming into a riot of fragrant purple trumpets in the spring. If you’ve never seen it, it has a sibling at the Seattle Japanese Garden in the Washington Park Arboretum. It’s like something out of a video game or an Ambien dream. To see it at its most splashy and ostentatious, one must visit an empress tree in late springtime.

So, when the bar goes, will the tree go? Ebrahimi said she had the same thought. A Stranger 2026 Genius Award nominee who’s been deemed Seattle’s Coolest Tree Expert , she estimates there are only about 30 empress trees in the city. “There’s one just a couple of blocks from [Vacilando], so part of me wonders if this one is a rogue tree that’s related.”

She adds that it’s one of the world’s fastest growing trees—growing up to 15 feet a year—and that in its native China, aristocratic families traditionally planted one when a baby girl was born so that it would mature alongside her and be ready to harvest when the family needed wood for a marriage dowry chest.

We began hatching a plan to try to save the empress, should the building face demolition. But where could it go? A container is a nonstarter—the empress tree grows so fast that it would become rootbound within weeks. It needs to live in the ground. Another issue: All signs point to empress trees not really tolerating their roots being disturbed. Its height and heft would be major obstacles to transplanting it as well. Maybe an arborist should be called? Could it survive a major pruning in order to bust it outta there? Carefully? If she can be moved, the empress tree at Vacilando ostensibly needs to live somewhere similar to a restaurant patio, where she grows from soil but drops her seeds over concrete.

To complicate matters, Washington state has had its little eyeball on this type of tree. The empress tree is really good at making more of itself, and it’s considered invasive in the Southwest and Eastern United States as such. Although it’s not officially considered a noxious weed here in Washington, it’s on the monitor list. Not a great situation for an imminently homeless tree.

Terrified that this beloved empress will be left behind to get crunched up along with the building, I fired off an email to Bar Vacilando’s parent company, Black Bottle Group, to ask what’s in the works here. Their response didn’t answer my question, except it actually did, without saying so.

“Thank you so much for coming to Vacilando over the years, and for caring about the beloved tree. When we took the space over 10 years ago, it was a single sprout issuing out of the brick, about two feet high. We’ve pruned it every year, it must have some water source, it has an incredible life force that has given us nourishment in every way that only Nature can. Thank you for your kind words. We are so grateful.”
Oh no. This is the Lynchian atmospheric whooshing of emails. Something bad is about to happen in this movie.

The next afternoon, I fled to the bar to ask questions in person. Stranger photo director and queer regenerative farm cofounder Billie Winter met me there. The tree looked bigger and more fabulous than ever, and we gazed up at its majesty. “The property owner is a ghost,” our very busy server said when asked what the fate of the tree might be, adding that it’s technically part of the building next door—currently home to Grandad’s Barber Shop—and not the one that housed Vacilando. “No one knows. Someone will probably take care of it, though!” Big not-my-problem energy. I would feel the same way if it were my second-to-last day of my job with maybe no notice.

Per Capitol Hill Blog, the barber shop building that the empress tree grows out of is not on the chopping block, just the one to the south. It’s easy to imagine the empress getting damaged in the process, of course. Both buildings are owned by somewhat-renowned local architect Gerald Kumata, who is 83 years old and seemingly not readily contactable. Perhaps a literal ghost as well. I thought back to the sage words of Taha Ebrahimi. “Get a photo of the source tree,” she’d texted earlier. “I’m certain it’s the source! It’s only two blocks to the east on 17th just north of Harrison! It had to have blown over to Vacilando.”

It was there. It was massive and fully mature, at least double the height of Vacilando’s tree. And it had TONS of seed pods. Most were cracked open and empty, but I jumped into the sky and managed to grab hold of a branch with more pods on it and pull it down. Billie had brought a little jar to collect the dusty, insect-wing-like seeds that remained in the walnut-like shells. In they went. I accidentally broke the branch, but it had a green shoot on there, which Ebrahimi said we could hypothetically propagate. “It will grow like gangbusters,” she wrote. “If you can cut a green shoot off, grow it in a vase until it grows roots!” I wrapped a wet paper towel around the base and stuck the whole thing in a Ziploc. A passerby asked if we were foraging for food, and we excitedly rambled at them about the empress tree at Bar Vacilando and how we’re pretty sure we found the mother tree. They wanted to follow @treeswithtaha on the socials and we told them how. At press time, we don’t have any real answers. Taha Ebrahimi is thrilled to hear that she was probably right and it was a rogue empress after all. Farmer Billie has a slew of seeds from the mother tree and, I’m sure, can germinate them easily. The green shoot is in a pickle jar of water in my kitchen window. I’m trying to figure out how to same-day-ship some root hormone to get it started. We can rebuild. Still, it’d be nice to save that poor patio empress. It seems crass to think that whomever is in charge of redeveloping and/or leveling the building in question would just destroy this elegant fashion icon without thinking. But I suppose we shouldn’t put it past some real estate developers, among the Disney-villainest characters in the land, to kill a pretty tree for being in the way. I accept that I am not in control of the fate of the Vacilando Empress, but look. If something bad is in the pipeline for her and someone hears about it, please let me know @megvanhuygen and I’ll figure it out. Hell, I’ll reconstruct Bar Vacilando’s patio in my backyard if I have to, frame by frame. Whatever needs to be done. This tree is loved by so very many. We’ll all make it happen.
